tasks.prompt: Each autumn, a small plant on a forested watershed gets complaints about tea coloured water, and this year the colour survives the full treatment process into the clearwell.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario surface water plant; the watershed is heavily forested with wetlands. Records are from the fall log for training only.

evidence.label: A filtered lab sample of the raw water keeps its tea colour, reading 85 colour units after filtration.
Raw water colour rises every fall as leaves drop and wetlands drain into the creek.
Turbidity is low at 3 NTU, so the colour is not from suspended silt.
Coagulant dose increases reduce the colour only slightly at the current pH.
Chlorine demand is higher than usual and residuals fall faster in the clearwell.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The colour is true colour from dissolved natural organic matter washed from the forest and wetlands, which needs coagulation tuned for organics removal, not more filtration.
The colour is apparent colour from fine silt that the filters are failing to remove.
Rust from the plant's own piping is colouring the treated water.
Algae in the creek are producing the colour this fall.

inference.explanation: Colour that remains after lab filtration is true colour from dissolved organics, and the low turbidity rules out silt. The seasonal pattern tied to leaf fall and wetland drainage, plus higher chlorine demand from organics, fits dissolved natural organic matter. Rust or algae would not show this filtered sample result.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Run jar tests at several coagulant doses and pH values measuring filtered colour, to find conditions that remove the dissolved colour.
Inspect the plant piping for internal rust and tuberculation.
Count algae species in the raw water under the microscope.
Backwash the filters and measure colour across each unit.

nextClue.explanation: Jar tests that measure filtered colour across doses and pH show whether enhanced coagulation can remove the dissolved organics.

clueText.nc1: At a higher dose and slightly lower pH, filtered colour falls below 15 units, confirming dissolved organics removable by tuned coagulation.
clueText.nc2: Plant piping is clean coated steel with no rust source found.
clueText.nc3: Algae counts are low in the fall samples, so algae are not producing the colour.
clueText.nc4: Colour is unchanged across the filters, so filtration was never the step removing it.

tasks.prompt: Black water complaints arrive from across a small town over one weekend in October, and a sample from a hydrant comes out grey black before clearing.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario system supplied by a deep reservoir well field and a small storage reservoir; records are from the complaint log for training only.

evidence.label: The complaints started the week the reservoir surface temperature matched the bottom temperature and fall winds picked up.
A hydrant sample shows manganese at 0.9 mg/L, far above the usual 0.02 mg/L.
Iron in the same sample is normal and chlorine residuals are normal.
Black particles in the sample dissolve in acid and the water clears after flushing.
The same complaint pattern happened during turnover two years ago.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Reservoir turnover has mixed manganese rich bottom water through the supply, and the oxidized manganese is causing the black water.
A watermain has corroded through and soil is entering under pressure.
The plant's chlorine dose has tripled and is burning the manganese out of the pipes.
A fuel oil spill has reached the reservoir intake.

inference.explanation: The timing at turnover, very high manganese with normal iron, particles that behave like manganese oxide, and the same pattern in a past turnover year all point to turnover mixing. A break, a dose change, or a spill would not produce system wide manganese at these levels with normal residuals.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Sample manganese at the reservoir outlet and at several depths to confirm the mixed layer is uniform, and track it daily as the reservoir restratifies or is drawn down.
Excavate at the first complaint address to look for a corroded main.
Cut the chlorine dose and watch complaint rates.
Search the reservoir surface for an oil sheen by boat.

nextClue.explanation: Depth samples showing uniform manganese confirm turnover mixing as the source of the black water.

clueText.nc1: Manganese is uniformly high at all depths right after turnover and falls over two weeks, confirming the turnover explanation.
clueText.nc2: The main at the complaint address is sound when a nearby dig for other work exposes it.
clueText.nc3: Complaints fade as manganese falls, with no dose change made, so chlorine was not the driver.
clueText.nc4: No sheen or fuel odour is found anywhere on the reservoir.

tasks.prompt: Homes at the highest elevation in a small system report low pressure every evening between 6 and 9 pm, while the rest of town is fine.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario system with one ground level storage tank feeding a pressure zone that includes a hilltop street; records are for training only.

evidence.label: Evening complaints coincide with the storage tank reaching its lowest level of the day.
Plant discharge pressure is steady and the well pumps keep up overnight, refilling the tank by morning.
A pressure logger on the hilltop street shows pressure falling as tank level falls, then recovering overnight.
Daytime pressures on the hilltop are normal when the tank is full.
No new large water users have connected this year.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The hilltop homes sit so high relative to the tank that normal evening drawdown drops their pressure below comfortable levels.
The well pumps are undersized and cannot keep up with evening demand.
A partially closed valve is throttling the hilltop street all day.
The hilltop homes all have leaking plumbing that shows up in the evening.

inference.explanation: Pressure on the hilltop tracks tank level exactly and recovers when the tank refills, and the pumps do refill it overnight, so supply capacity is adequate. A throttled valve or home leaks would cause low pressure all day, not only at low tank level.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Log tank level and hilltop pressure together for three days and compare the pressure at full and low tank levels against the elevation difference.
Run both well pumps together one evening and watch hilltop pressure.
Sound the hilltop feed main for a partly closed valve by checking flow at two hydrants.
Meter one complaining home overnight for leak flow.

nextClue.explanation: Paired level and pressure logging shows whether the evening loss matches the elevation head lost as the tank draws down.

clueText.nc1: Hilltop pressure falls by almost exactly the tank drawdown head each evening and recovers on refill, confirming elevation and tank level as the cause.
clueText.nc2: Running both pumps helps only while the tank is being refilled, matching the level explanation rather than pump size.
clueText.nc3: Hydrant flows on the hilltop feed are normal when the tank is full, so no valve is throttling the street.
clueText.nc4: The metered home shows no overnight leak flow.

tasks.prompt: Several homes in a newer subdivision report blue green stains on fixtures and two have had pinhole leaks in copper plumbing, and the water is from a low alkalinity well supply.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario groundwater system; the well water is soft with low alkalinity and the plant does not adjust pH. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: Treated water pH is 6.6 and alkalinity is 25 mg/L as CaCO3.
First draw samples in affected homes show copper well above the aesthetic objective, while flushed samples are much lower.
The stains and leaks are worst in homes with the longest copper runs.
Chlorine residuals and bacteriological results are normal across the system.
Homes with plastic plumbing in the same subdivision report no staining.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The low pH, low alkalinity water is corrosive to copper plumbing, dissolving copper during standing time in the pipes.
The well water naturally contains high copper from the aquifer rock.
The chlorine dose is dissolving the copper pipes.
Faulty flux used by one builder is causing all the staining and leaks.

inference.explanation: First draw copper far above flushed samples shows the copper comes from the household plumbing during standing time, not from the well. Low pH and low alkalinity make the water corrosive, plastic plumbed homes are unaffected, and disinfection is normal, which rules out aquifer copper, chlorine attack, and a single builder's flux.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Collect paired first draw and flushed copper samples at several homes and compare them with the treated water pH and alkalinity record.
Sample the raw well water for copper before any treatment.
Cut the chlorine dose for a month and resample the homes.
Survey which builder built each affected home.

nextClue.explanation: Paired first draw and flushed samples, read against the corrosive water chemistry, confirm whether copper is picked up in home plumbing.

clueText.nc1: First draw copper is high and flushed copper is low at every home, while raw well copper is near zero, confirming corrosion of household copper by the low pH, low alkalinity water.
clueText.nc2: Raw well copper is near zero, so the aquifer is not the source.
clueText.nc3: Staining continues at the lower dose in a later check, so chlorine was not the cause.
clueText.nc4: Affected homes were built by three different builders, so one builder's flux does not explain it.

tasks.prompt: Homes within a few streets of the plant complain of strong chlorine taste, while the far end of town barely holds its minimum residual, and both patterns have existed for months.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario distribution system, long and narrow along a lakeshore road; records are from the sampling log for training only.

evidence.label: Free chlorine is 1.6 mg/L two streets from the plant and 0.15 mg/L at the far end.
The plant doses to meet the far end minimum, raising the dose over the years.
There is no booster chlorination station anywhere in the system.
Water takes about three days to travel from the plant to the far end in summer.
Bacteriological results are compliant everywhere, including the far end.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The single dosing point cannot serve both ends of a long system: near homes get the high fresh dose while the far end loses residual over its three day travel time.
The plant chlorinator is malfunctioning and dosing unevenly hour to hour.
Near plant homes have oversensitive taste because of a local plumbing issue.
The far end samples are being taken incorrectly and residuals there are actually fine.

inference.explanation: The smooth gradient from high near the plant to low at the far end, the three day travel time, and the history of raising the single dose to protect the far end all fit a one point dosing problem on a long system. An erratic chlorinator would show swings in time, not a steady distance gradient.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Profile free chlorine at six points along the lakeshore road on the same morning to map the residual gradient.
Log the chlorinator output hourly for a week to look for swings.
Inspect plumbing at two near plant homes for taste causes.
Retrain the sampler and resample the far end once.

nextClue.explanation: A same morning profile along the road shows the distance based gradient that a single dosing point produces.

clueText.nc1: The profile falls smoothly from 1.6 mg/L near the plant to 0.15 mg/L at the far end, confirming travel time decay from a single dosing point.
clueText.nc2: Chlorinator output is steady hour to hour all week, so dosing is not erratic.
clueText.nc3: Plumbing at the near homes is standard and the taste matches their measured 1.6 mg/L residual.
clueText.nc4: Careful resampling reproduces the low far end residual, so sampling error was not the cause.

tasks.prompt: A small plant's treated water leaves the filters with a good chlorine residual, but water leaving the clearwell is 0.4 mg/L lower, and the loss is worst after sunny weekends.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant with an uncovered clearwell section built decades ago and a newer covered cell; records are for training only.

evidence.label: Residual entering the clearwell is 1.2 mg/L and leaving is 0.8 mg/L on weekdays, 0.6 mg/L after sunny weekends.
The older clearwell cell is uncovered and open to sunlight.
Green algae growth is visible on the walls of the uncovered cell.
The covered cell, tested on its own, shows almost no residual loss.
Clearwell temperature rises in the sun over weekends when flows are low.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Sunlight and algae growth in the uncovered clearwell cell are destroying chlorine, and low weekend flows give the water more time in that cell.
The clearwell baffles have failed and water short circuits in minutes.
A crack in the clearwell floor is leaking chlorinated water into the ground.
The chlorine analyzer at the clearwell outlet needs calibration.

inference.explanation: The loss is larger after sunny low flow weekends, the uncovered cell has algae and sun exposure, and the covered cell loses almost nothing. Short circuiting would cut contact time but not destroy chlorine this way, a floor leak would not depend on sunshine, and the covered cell comparison rules out a bad analyzer.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Sample residual entering and leaving each clearwell cell separately on a sunny low flow day.
Run a dye trace through the clearwell to check for short circuiting.
Compare clearwell level drop overnight against pumped volumes to look for leakage.
Calibrate the outlet analyzer against a bench DPD test.

nextClue.explanation: Sampling each cell separately on a sunny day isolates whether the uncovered cell is where the chlorine is lost.

clueText.nc1: The uncovered cell loses 0.5 mg/L while the covered cell loses 0.05 mg/L on the same day, confirming sunlight and algae in the open cell as the cause.
clueText.nc2: The dye trace shows reasonable travel time through the cells, so severe short circuiting is not present.
clueText.nc3: Overnight level and pumped volumes balance, so the floor is not leaking.
clueText.nc4: The bench DPD test matches the analyzer, so the readings are accurate.

tasks.prompt: After backwashes, an operator at a small plant finds sand media in the backwash waste trough discharge and the filter bed surface is becoming uneven.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario dual media filter plant; the air scour system was retuned by a contractor last month. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: Media is found in the waste stream mainly during the combined air and water wash stage.
The bed surface shows mounds and low spots after washing.
Air scour flow was increased during the contractor's retune to improve cleaning.
Effluent turbidity is still good, but bed depth at the low spots is 80 mm below design.
The underdrain nozzles were inspected two years ago and were sound.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The increased air scour rate is too aggressive and is carrying media over into the waste troughs during the combined wash.
The underdrains have failed and media is escaping downward into the clearwell.
The media has dissolved in the treated water over time.
Backwash water flow alone, at its normal rate, is washing the media out.

inference.explanation: Media loss occurs during the air scour stage, began after the air rate was raised, and the bed is being thrown into mounds, which fits overly aggressive air scour. Downward loss through underdrains would show in the clearwell instead, and the water only wash rate is unchanged and normal.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Reduce the air scour rate to the design value for one wash and inspect the waste stream and bed surface afterward.
Take a clearwell sample and settle it to look for media grains.
Assay a media sample for acid solubility.
Raise the water wash rate alone and watch the waste stream.

nextClue.explanation: One wash at the design air rate shows directly whether the higher air scour was carrying media out.

clueText.nc1: At the design air rate no media appears in the waste and the bed levels out over several washes, confirming the excessive air scour rate.
clueText.nc2: The settled clearwell sample contains no media grains, so media is not escaping downward.
clueText.nc3: The media assay shows normal low solubility, so it is not dissolving.
clueText.nc4: The water only wash at normal rate carries no media into the troughs.

tasks.prompt: On a bitterly cold, windy night, a small lake intake plant loses raw water flow twice, and each time flow returns after the crew steams the intake crib area.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario lake intake with a shallow crib in an exposed bay; records are from the night shift log for training only.

evidence.label: Flow losses happen on the coldest, windiest nights when the lake is still open water.
Divers later find slush ice packed around the crib bars, not solid sheet ice.
The lake surface has no solid ice cover yet this season.
Raw water temperature at the intake is at 0 degrees C and slightly supercooled on those nights.
Flow recovers fully after steaming and stays normal on calmer cold nights.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Frazil ice crystals forming in the supercooled open water are sticking to the crib and choking the intake on windy nights.
A solid ice sheet has formed over the crib and sealed it off.
The raw water pump is losing prime because of the cold.
Zebra mussels have suddenly blocked the crib bars.

inference.explanation: Slush ice on the bars, supercooled open water, losses only on windy pre freeze up nights, and recovery after steaming are the classic signs of frazil ice. There is no solid sheet yet, the pump works once flow is restored, and mussels do not appear and vanish overnight with the weather.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Log intake flow, wind, and raw water temperature through the next cold windy night and inspect the crib by camera at the time flow drops.
Break up surface ice over the crib with an ice crew.
Reprime the raw pump and check its suction line for cold damage.
Schedule a mussel scraping dive for the spring.

nextClue.explanation: Camera inspection at the moment flow falls, tied to wind and temperature, confirms whether frazil slush is packing the crib.

clueText.nc1: The camera shows slush ice building on the bars as supercooled water flows past on the windy night, confirming frazil ice blockage.
clueText.nc2: There is still no solid sheet to break, so sheet ice was not the blockage.
clueText.nc3: The pump holds prime and delivers full flow whenever the crib is clear, so the pump is not the problem.
clueText.nc4: The bars show only light mussel growth, far too little to choke flow overnight.

tasks.prompt: Every spring, a small plant on a soft water lake struggles for two weeks: floc will not form properly even though turbidity is only moderate, and the water is at its coldest.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario shield lake plant; spring melt brings dilute, cold, low alkalinity water. Records are from three springs of logs for training only.

evidence.label: Raw water temperature is 1 to 2 degrees C during the problem weeks.
Raw alkalinity drops to 12 mg/L as CaCO3 during melt dilution.
Jar tests at bench temperature form floc, but jars kept at raw water temperature form poor floc at the same dose.
Increasing rapid mix energy in the jar tests improves floc at cold temperature.
The same problems repeat every spring and resolve as the lake warms.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Cold, dilute melt water slows coagulation reactions and, with very low alkalinity, makes floc formation poor until dose and mixing are adjusted for spring conditions.
The alum feed pump loses capacity every spring and recovers by summer.
Spring runoff carries a chemical that permanently destroys alum.
The flocculation basin has a structural short circuit that appears in spring.

inference.explanation: The problem repeats only in the coldest, most dilute weeks, cold jar tests reproduce it while warm jars do not, and extra mixing energy helps, all of which fit cold water kinetics plus low alkalinity. A seasonal pump failure, a mystery chemical, or a structural fault would not track temperature and dilution so closely.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Run a spring jar test matrix at raw water temperature varying alum dose, alkalinity addition, and mix energy to set spring operating conditions.
Test the alum pump output each week through the spring.
Send raw water for a full organic chemical scan during melt.
Dye test the flocculation basin for short circuiting.

nextClue.explanation: A cold temperature jar matrix shows which combination of dose, alkalinity, and mixing restores floc under actual spring conditions.

clueText.nc1: Cold jars need more alum, added alkalinity, and stronger mixing to form good floc, confirming cold dilute water chemistry as the cause.
clueText.nc2: The pump delivers its set rate all spring, so feed capacity is not seasonal.
clueText.nc3: The chemical scan finds nothing unusual in the melt water.
clueText.nc4: The dye test shows even flow through the flocculation basin.

tasks.prompt: One routine distribution sample from a community hall tap comes back total coliform positive, and the operator must decide whether the system or the sample site is the problem.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario distribution system; the hall tap is a kitchen faucet with an aerator and a spray hose. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: The positive sample came from a kitchen tap fitted with an aerator and a detachable spray hose.
Free chlorine at the hall that day was 0.7 mg/L, and at neighbouring sites 0.6 to 0.8 mg/L.
Repeat samples taken the next day from the hall's outside tap and two nearby homes are all absent for total coliform.
No pressure loss, main break, or repair happened in that area that week.
The hall custodian reports the kitchen tap is rarely used and the hose sits in the sink.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The positive result most likely came from contamination at the sample tap itself, the aerator and hose in a rarely used sink, rather than from the distribution water.
The distribution system has widespread coliform contamination that repeats missed.
A main break that week let soil bacteria into the pipes.
The laboratory contaminated the sample bottle during analysis.

inference.explanation: Good residuals everywhere, clean repeats from proper sampling taps nearby, no pressure event, and a poor sampling tap with an aerator, a hose sitting in a sink, and long stagnation all point to the sample site. Widespread contamination or a break would show in the repeats and residuals.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Take repeat samples from the dedicated sampling tap after removing the aerator and flushing, alongside upstream and downstream sites, as the sampling protocol requires.
Issue a boil water advisory for the whole system until further notice.
Excavate the main in front of the hall to look for a break.
Ask the laboratory to reanalyze the original bottle.

nextClue.explanation: Proper repeat sampling at the site and its neighbours, following the protocol, distinguishes a tap problem from a system problem.

clueText.nc1: All repeats from the cleaned dedicated tap and neighbouring sites are absent, with residuals normal, confirming the original positive came from the sample tap conditions.
clueText.nc2: An advisory is not supported once repeats are clean and residuals were always normal.
clueText.nc3: The main is intact and there was never a pressure loss to investigate by excavation.
clueText.nc4: The original bottle cannot be reanalyzed after its hold time, and the clean repeats answer the question directly.

tasks.prompt: A small plant finds it needs more and more sodium hypochlorite each week to hold the same residual, and the day tank was filled from a bulk delivery two months ago at the start of a hot summer.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant storing bulk hypochlorite in an uninsulated room that gets hot in summer; records are for training only.

evidence.label: The bulk tank sits in a room that reaches 32 degrees C on summer afternoons.
A titration of the bulk tank shows available chlorine at 7 percent, down from 12.5 percent at delivery.
Chlorine demand of the treated water is unchanged from spring.
The feed pump output was verified with a calibration column and is accurate.
A fresh pail of hypochlorite at the same pump setting restores the residual at once.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The stored hypochlorite has degraded in the heat over two months, so each litre delivers less chlorine than the feed settings assume.
The treated water demand has tripled, though the lab demand tests say otherwise.
The feed pump is wearing out and pumping less each week.
The chlorine analyzer has drifted and the residual is actually fine.

inference.explanation: The titration proves the chemical itself lost strength, the hot storage explains the decay, demand tests are unchanged, the pump is verified accurate, and fresh chemical restores residual at the same settings. That combination rules out demand, pump wear, and analyzer drift.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Titrate the bulk tank weekly and compare feed rates needed before and after a fresh delivery to confirm the strength loss pattern.
Run chlorine demand tests on treated water daily for a week.
Replace the feed pump and compare residuals.
Recalibrate the analyzer and compare with bench tests.

nextClue.explanation: Titrating the stored chemical and watching the feed rate change with fresh stock confirms degradation as the cause.

clueText.nc1: The fresh delivery titrates at 12.4 percent and the required feed rate drops back to normal at once, confirming the old stock had degraded in the heat.
clueText.nc2: Demand tests stay flat all week, so the water was not consuming more chlorine.
clueText.nc3: The original pump holds the residual on fresh chemical, so it was not wearing out.
clueText.nc4: Bench tests matched the analyzer throughout, so its readings were true.

tasks.prompt: The online chlorine analyzer at a small plant reads 0.3 mg/L, but the operator's bench DPD test on a grab sample from the same tap reads 1.0 mg/L, matching yesterday's results.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant with a reagent based online analyzer fed by a small sample line; records are for training only.

evidence.label: Bench DPD tests by two operators both read 1.0 mg/L on fresh grabs.
The analyzer sample line flow is a trickle compared with its normal stream.
A piece of scale is visible in the analyzer sample line strainer.
The analyzer reagents are within their expiry date and were changed last month.
Distribution residuals measured today are normal at all sites.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The analyzer is reading low because its sample line is partly blocked by scale, so it is testing stale water, not because the plant residual is low.
The plant residual really is 0.3 mg/L and both bench tests are wrong.
The bench DPD reagent has gone bad and reads high on every sample.
The clearwell chlorine has stratified so different taps give different water.

inference.explanation: Two bench tests agree with each other and with normal distribution results, while the analyzer's sample flow is a trickle with scale in its strainer, which means it is measuring old water sitting in the line. Bad bench reagent or stratification would not explain the blocked sample line or the consistent field results.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Clean the sample line strainer, restore full sample flow, and compare the analyzer with a bench test on the same water.
Raise the plant chlorine dose until the analyzer reads 1.0 mg/L.
Replace the bench DPD reagent and retest the grab sample.
Sample the clearwell at several depths for chlorine.

nextClue.explanation: Restoring the sample flow and comparing instruments on the same water directly tests the stale sample explanation.

clueText.nc1: With the strainer cleaned, the analyzer climbs to 0.98 mg/L and matches the bench test, confirming the blocked sample line caused the low reading.
clueText.nc2: Raising the dose would have pushed the true 1.0 mg/L residual far too high, which the bench tests warned against.
clueText.nc3: The bench reagent reads correctly on a standard solution, so it was not reading high.
clueText.nc4: Clearwell samples are uniform with depth, so stratification was not occurring.

tasks.prompt: Residents near a booster station report loud banging in their pipes right after the station pumps start, and one home has had a water heater relief valve weep after starts.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario booster station with a fast closing check valve on each pump; records are from the complaint log for training only.

evidence.label: The banging happens within seconds of a pump start, never at other times.
A pressure logger near the station records a brief spike to 950 kPa right after starts, against a normal 550 kPa.
The pump check valves are swing type and slam audibly at the station on shutdown as well.
Pipe supports in the station are rattling loose over time.
Steady state pressures and flows are normal once the start transient passes.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Fast pump starts and slamming check valves are creating water hammer pressure transients that travel into the nearby homes.
The station is running at too high a steady pressure all day.
Air in the residents' plumbing is causing the banging at random times.
The water heater relief valves in the area are all defective.

inference.explanation: The bangs are locked to pump starts, the logger catches a large brief spike at exactly those moments, the check valves slam audibly, and steady pressures are normal. That is the signature of water hammer, not high steady pressure, random air, or a batch of faulty relief valves.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Record pressure at high speed logging through several pump starts, then trial a slower valve closure or soft start setting and log again.
Lower the station steady discharge pressure by 100 kPa for a week.
Bleed air from the highest home's plumbing.
Replace the relief valve at the complaining home.

nextClue.explanation: High speed pressure logging through starts, before and after slowing the transient, confirms water hammer and whether the fix works.

clueText.nc1: Spikes of about 400 kPa above normal appear at each start and shrink to under 80 kPa with the softened start, confirming water hammer from the fast transient.
clueText.nc2: Steady pressure was already normal, so lowering it would not remove the start spikes.
clueText.nc3: No air is found at the home's taps, and the banging stays tied to pump starts.
clueText.nc4: The relief valve tests at its set pressure, so it was responding to real spikes, not failing.

tasks.prompt: During fire flow testing, one hydrant in an older part of town delivers far less flow than its twin on the next street, though static pressure at both is the same.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario distribution system with gate valves on each street corner; records are from the flow test day for training only.

evidence.label: Static pressure is 480 kPa at both hydrants.
The weak hydrant's flow improves partway through the test, then falls again.
A valve on the weak hydrant's street was operated during a repair two months ago and its position was not recorded.
The twin hydrant on the parallel street flows at full expected rate.
No leaks are visible and the rest of the area tests normally.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: A gate valve on the weak hydrant's street was left partly closed after the repair, throttling flow while static pressure still recovers.
The weak hydrant's barrel is blocked with stones and debris.
The main feeding that street has collapsed internally.
The whole older area is undersupplied by the plant at test times.

inference.explanation: Equal static pressure with poor flow is the classic sign of a restriction that only shows under flow, and the unrecorded valve operation after the repair is the obvious suspect. Debris in one hydrant would not fit flow improving mid test, and the twin hydrant and the rest of the area perform normally.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Locate the street's gate valves and count turns to fully open on each, then repeat the hydrant flow test.
Remove the hydrant bonnet and clear its barrel.
Excavate the street main to check for collapse.
Repeat the test at night when plant demand is low.

nextClue.explanation: Counting valve turns and retesting flow directly checks for a partly closed valve throttling the street.

clueText.nc1: One valve takes six extra turns to full open, and the hydrant then flows at the expected rate, confirming the valve had been left partly closed.
clueText.nc2: The hydrant barrel is clear when inspected afterward.
clueText.nc3: The main is sound, as shown by the restored flow without any excavation.
clueText.nc4: Night testing was unnecessary once the valve was found, and static pressure had never suggested a supply shortage.

tasks.prompt: A small system's elevated tank overflows twice in one week, both times at night, though the well pumps are set to stop at the normal high level.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario system with level control by a float and pressure sensor at the tank; records are for training only.

evidence.label: The altitude valve and pump controls work correctly when tested by hand.
The level sensor reading freezes at one value for hours in the SCADA trend, then jumps.
Biofilm and slime are found coating the submerged level sensor when it is pulled.
Overflows happen on low demand nights when the tank fills slowly.
The tank level sight gauge shows a higher level than the sensor reported before each overflow.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The fouled level sensor is under reading the true level, so the pumps keep filling past the high level setpoint at night.
The well pumps have become too powerful and fill the tank faster than controls can react.
Night demand has collapsed because a large user closed.
The overflow pipe is partly blocked, making normal filling look like overflow.

inference.explanation: A sensor trend that freezes and jumps, slime coating on the sensor, and a sight gauge reading higher than the sensor all show the level signal is wrong. Hand tests prove the controls and valve work, and slow night filling would make a working control system more accurate, not less.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Clean and test the level sensor against the sight gauge across a full fill cycle while logging both readings.
Throttle one well pump's discharge valve to slow filling.
Survey large users for a closure that cut night demand.
Rod out the overflow pipe.

nextClue.explanation: Comparing the cleaned sensor with the sight gauge over a fill cycle verifies whether the sensor now tracks true level and stops the pumps on time.

clueText.nc1: After cleaning, the sensor tracks the sight gauge within centimetres and the pumps stop at setpoint, confirming sensor fouling caused the overflows.
clueText.nc2: Filling rate was never the issue, since the controls now stop the same pumps correctly.
clueText.nc3: Night demand is unchanged from last year in the billing records.
clueText.nc4: The overflow pipe runs clear, and water only reached it when the tank was genuinely overfilled.

tasks.prompt: Over two years, a small town well needs longer pumping to meet the same demand, and its pumping water level has dropped 6 m while the static level is nearly unchanged.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario groundwater well in a sand and gravel aquifer, screened at 30 m; records are from the well log for training only.

evidence.label: Static water level in the well is almost the same as five years ago.
Pumping level drops much faster and lower than it used to at the same rate.
Specific capacity has fallen from 4.2 to 1.8 L/s per metre of drawdown.
Sand content in the discharge is unchanged and the water quality is stable.
Neighbouring wells in the same aquifer show no regional level decline.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The well screen and gravel pack are gradually encrusting and clogging, adding drawdown inside the well while the aquifer itself is healthy.
The aquifer is being mined and is running out of water.
The pump impellers are worn and can no longer lift the water.
A new large user nearby is drawing down the whole aquifer.

inference.explanation: Static level and neighbouring wells show the aquifer is fine, while the growing gap between static and pumping levels and the falling specific capacity point to losses at the screen and pack. Worn impellers would cut discharge pressure and flow, not create extra drawdown measured in the well.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Run a step drawdown test at several rates and compare well loss with aquifer loss against the well's original test.
Measure static levels in three neighbouring wells over a month.
Pull the pump and measure impeller clearances.
Meter the suspected large user's consumption.

nextClue.explanation: A step drawdown test separates aquifer loss from well loss, showing whether the extra drawdown is happening at the screen.

clueText.nc1: Well loss has tripled since the original test while aquifer loss is unchanged, confirming screen and pack encrustation as the cause.
clueText.nc2: Neighbouring static levels are stable, so there is no regional decline to explain the change.
clueText.nc3: The pump delivers its rated curve when tested, so impeller wear is not the cause.
clueText.nc4: No new large user exists on the service records for the area.

tasks.prompt: A well that has run clear for years suddenly pumps fine sand, and the sand separator fills within a day instead of a month.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario groundwater well with a manufactured screen in a fine sand aquifer; the pump was recently replaced with a higher capacity unit. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: Sand appeared within a week of the larger replacement pump being installed.
The new pump's rate is 30 percent above the well's original tested yield.
Sand grains match the aquifer sand size that the screen was designed to hold back at design velocity.
Static and pumping levels are normal and the water is otherwise clear of iron and colour.
Sand production is worst right after each pump start.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The oversized pump is pulling water through the screen faster than its design velocity, dragging aquifer sand through the slots.
The screen has corroded through in several places at once.
The aquifer itself has changed to a sandier layer this year.
The sand separator has failed and is recirculating trapped sand.

inference.explanation: Sand starting right after the bigger pump went in, a rate well above the tested yield, grains that the screen holds back only at design velocity, and surges at startup all point to excessive entrance velocity. A sudden multi point screen failure or an aquifer change would not be timed to the pump swap.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Throttle the pump back to the well's original tested rate for one week and log sand separator accumulation daily.
Run a downhole camera survey of the screen looking for corrosion holes.
Sample the aquifer from a test hole beside the well.
Replace the sand separator with a larger unit.

nextClue.explanation: Running at the original rate for a week shows whether sand production falls back to normal at design screen velocity.

clueText.nc1: At the original rate the separator takes a month to fill again, confirming the oversized pump's entrance velocity was dragging sand through the screen.
clueText.nc2: The camera survey shows the screen intact with no corrosion holes.
clueText.nc3: The test hole shows the same sand the well has always drawn from.
clueText.nc4: The separator was working correctly; it was simply receiving far more sand than design.

tasks.prompt: A shallow well near a busy highway shows chloride climbing every winter, reaching 240 mg/L in February, then slowly falling through the summer.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario groundwater system; the well is 60 m down gradient of a highway winter maintenance yard's snow dump. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: Chloride peaks each February and March, after the heaviest road salting months.
Sodium rises in step with chloride in the well samples.
A deeper well on the same property shows much lower chloride year round.
Chloride in the shallow well has trended upward over five winters.
No septic systems or farms are located between the highway yard and the well.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Road salt from the highway and its snow storage area is migrating through the shallow groundwater to the well each winter.
A leaking underground fuel tank at the yard is contaminating the well.
The laboratory is contaminating the chloride samples with salt from gloves.
Natural brine from deep rock is rising into the well every winter.

inference.explanation: The seasonal peak after salting, sodium rising with chloride, the shallow well affected while the deep well is not, and the five year upward trend all fit road salt moving through shallow groundwater. Fuel would not raise chloride and sodium together, lab contamination would not follow seasons, and deep brine would affect the deep well more, not less.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Sample chloride monthly at the shallow well, the deep well, and a monitoring point between the snow dump and the well for one winter.
Sample the shallow well for petroleum hydrocarbons.
Ask the lab to run blank samples with each batch.
Log deep rock brine indicators such as bromide in both wells.

nextClue.explanation: A line of monitoring points between the snow dump and the well shows whether a chloride plume is moving from the yard toward the well.

clueText.nc1: Chloride is highest at the monitoring point by the snow dump and falls toward the well, confirming road salt migration through the shallow aquifer.
clueText.nc2: Petroleum results are non detect, so a fuel leak is not affecting the well.
clueText.nc3: Lab blanks are clean, so sample contamination is ruled out.
clueText.nc4: Bromide stays low in both wells, so deep brine is not rising into the shallow well.

tasks.prompt: After a planned main repair and recharge, several homes report milky white water that clears from the bottom up in a glass within a minute.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario distribution system; the repaired section was drained and refilled the same morning. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: The milky water appeared the morning after the repaired main was refilled.
A glass of the water clears from the bottom upward in about a minute, leaving no residue.
Chlorine residuals and bacteriological samples in the area are normal.
Complaints fade over two days with no action beyond normal water use.
No sediment or particles settle out of the milky water.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The cloudiness is tiny air bubbles released from solution after the pressure changes of draining and refilling the main, and it is harmless and temporary.
White sediment from pipe scale is washing through the homes' plumbing.
The repair introduced a chemical contaminant that is precipitating in the water.
The plant has started sending out partially treated water.

inference.explanation: Water that clears from the bottom up with no residue is full of microbubbles rising and escaping, the classic sign of dissolved air after pressure changes. Sediment or precipitate would settle downward and leave residue, and the normal lab results and quick fade rule out a treatment or contamination problem.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Collect a sample in a clear glass at a complaining home and observe the clearing direction, and check a hydrant sample for the same effect.
Filter a litre of the water and weigh any residue collected.
Send a sample for a full chemical contamination scan.
Take treated water turbidity samples at the plant every hour for a day.

nextClue.explanation: The glass test at the home, repeated at a hydrant, confirms whether the cloudiness behaves like air bubbles rather than solids.

clueText.nc1: Both the home and hydrant samples clear from the bottom up with no residue, confirming dissolved air from the main recharge as the cause.
clueText.nc2: The filter collects no measurable residue, so white sediment is not present.
clueText.nc3: The chemical scan comes back unremarkable for the affected area.
clueText.nc4: Plant turbidity stays at 0.05 NTU all day, so partially treated water was not sent out.

tasks.prompt: A small plant's treated water aluminum has crept above the operational guideline for a month, and the operator notes it began after the alum dose was raised for a turbidity event and never lowered.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario surface water plant using alum coagulation; records are from the monthly lab reports for training only.

evidence.label: Treated aluminum rose in the same month the alum dose was increased by half.
Settled and treated pH sit at 6.0, below the plant's usual 6.8 to 7.2 range.
Raw water aluminum is low and unchanged.
Treated turbidity is excellent, better than the plant needs.
Jar tests at a lower alum dose and pH near 7 show good floc and much lower aluminum in the filtered water.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Excess alum dose at low pH is leaving dissolved aluminum in the treated water, because aluminum solubility rises as pH falls away from its minimum near neutral.
The raw water has developed a natural aluminum problem from the watershed.
The filters are shedding their media coating into the water.
The lab's aluminum method has drifted high this month.

inference.explanation: The rise tracks the dose increase, the pH is low where aluminum stays dissolved, raw aluminum is unchanged, and jar tests fix the problem by lowering dose and restoring pH. That rules out a watershed change, media shedding, and lab drift.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Run jar tests across dose and pH to pick settings that hold turbidity and minimize filtered aluminum, then trial them at the plant for a week.
Sample raw water aluminum at the intake weekly for a month.
Inspect a filter bed for coating loss.
Send split samples to a second laboratory for aluminum.

nextClue.explanation: Jar tests that vary dose and pH together find the operating point where aluminum carryover is lowest while turbidity stays good.

clueText.nc1: At the lower dose and pH near 7, filtered aluminum falls well under the guideline with turbidity still excellent, confirming excess alum at low pH as the cause.
clueText.nc2: Raw aluminum stays low all month, so the watershed is not the source.
clueText.nc3: The bed coating is intact and even across the filter.
clueText.nc4: The second laboratory agrees with the first on the high samples, so the results were real.

tasks.prompt: Filtered turbidity from a small two filter plant spikes each time one filter is taken out for backwash, even though the backwashed filter itself performs well.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant where total plant flow stays constant while one of two filters is washed; records are for training only.

evidence.label: When one filter is offline, the running filter's flow doubles to carry the full plant flow.
The turbidity spike on the running filter begins within minutes of the other unit going offline.
The spike fades once both filters are back in service at shared flow.
Settled water turbidity is steady through these events.
The running filter's media and underdrains were inspected this year and are sound.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Doubling the filtration rate on the remaining filter is shearing captured floc through the bed and causing the turbidity spikes.
The backwash process is contaminating the running filter through a leaking valve.
The settled water quality collapses whenever a filter is washed.
The turbidimeter cell gets air bubbles during backwashes and reads falsely high.

inference.explanation: The spike is tied to the period when one filter carries double rate, begins and ends with that condition, and settled water is steady. Rate surge shearing floc through the bed fits all of that, while a leaking valve, a settling collapse, or meter bubbles would not track the flow split so exactly.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Reduce total plant flow by half during the next backwash so the running filter keeps its normal rate, and log its effluent turbidity.
Pressure test the backwash waste valve for leakage into the running filter.
Log settled water turbidity through a full backwash cycle.
Watch the turbidimeter sample line for bubbles during a backwash.

nextClue.explanation: Holding the running filter at its normal rate during a wash is the direct test of the rate surge explanation.

clueText.nc1: With plant flow halved during the wash, the running filter's turbidity stays flat, confirming that the doubled rate was shearing floc through the bed.
clueText.nc2: The waste valve holds pressure with no leakage found.
clueText.nc3: Settled turbidity stays steady through the whole cycle, so settling was not collapsing.
clueText.nc4: The sample line runs bubble free while the spike occurs at full rate.

tasks.prompt: A soda ash silo feeder at a small plant keeps showing a running motor but the pH of the treated water drifts down for hours until staff bang on the silo cone and flow resumes.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant feeding dry soda ash for alkalinity; the silo is in a humid pumphouse. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: Banging the silo cone restores chemical flow every time.
The soda ash in the cone is found caked and clumped when the inspection hatch is opened.
The feeder screw and motor test at full rated output when the cone flows freely.
Humidity in the pumphouse is high and condensation forms on the silo walls.
pH drift episodes have become more frequent during a humid summer.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Moisture is caking the soda ash so it bridges over the feeder outlet, starving the feed until the bridge is knocked loose.
The feeder motor is failing intermittently and stopping under load.
The pH probe is drifting and the chemical feed is actually steady.
The soda ash supply itself is a bad batch with no alkalinity value.

inference.explanation: Flow restored by banging the cone, caked clumps found at the outlet, a feeder that tests at full output when material flows, and humid conditions all fit bridging from moisture. A failing motor would not respond to banging, probe drift would not match the caked material, and a bad batch would not flow and work after each knock.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Weigh feeder output over 30 minutes before and after clearing the cone, and log pumphouse humidity against feed interruptions for two weeks.
Run the feeder motor on a test bench under load.
Compare the pH probe against grab sample titrations for a day.
Assay the soda ash from the silo for alkalinity content.

nextClue.explanation: Timed feeder output weights plus a humidity log show whether feed stops when moisture cakes the cone.

clueText.nc1: Output is zero while bridged, full rate once the cone is cleared, and interruptions cluster on the most humid days, confirming moisture bridging.
clueText.nc2: The motor performs normally under bench load.
clueText.nc3: Grab titrations match the probe, so the pH drift was real.
clueText.nc4: The soda ash assays at full strength, so the batch is good.

tasks.prompt: The alum day tank at a small plant is losing level about twice as fast as the feed pump's set rate can explain, and the operator finds the containment floor damp each morning.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario surface water plant with a day tank inside a containment curb; records are for training only.

evidence.label: Measured pump output with a calibration column matches the set rate.
The tank level falls even during a night when the plant and feed pump were off.
A dye coloured wet trail runs from a cracked fitting on the tank outlet line into the containment sump.
The containment sump liquid tests as diluted alum.
No chemical is found outside the containment area.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: A cracked fitting on the day tank outlet line is leaking alum into containment, which explains both the level loss and the damp floor.
The feed pump is secretly delivering twice its set rate to the process.
Plant staff are drawing alum for another use without logging it.
The tank level gauge is faulty and no chemical is actually being lost.

inference.explanation: Level falling while the pump is off rules out overfeeding, the calibration column confirms the pump rate, and the dyed trail plus alum in the sump prove a leak at the outlet fitting. A faulty gauge cannot put real alum in the sump or wet the floor.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Isolate and pressure test the outlet line section, then repair the fitting and compare tank level loss against pump rate for three days.
Recalibrate the feed pump at several speeds.
Audit chemical use logs against delivery volumes.
Replace the level gauge and watch the tank for a week.

nextClue.explanation: Pressure testing the outlet line locates the leak, and post repair level accounting confirms the loss has stopped.

clueText.nc1: The line section fails the pressure test at the cracked fitting, and after repair the tank loss matches the pump rate exactly, confirming the leak.
clueText.nc2: The pump calibration was already correct at all speeds.
clueText.nc3: Use logs and deliveries balance once the leaked volume is counted.
clueText.nc4: The original gauge reads correctly against a manual dip after the repair.

tasks.prompt: In a subdivision built in phases, only the newest phase at the far end has chronic low chlorine residuals, while older phases closer to the plant are always fine.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario distribution system; the newest phase has large mains sized for future growth but few homes connected so far. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: The newest phase mains are oversized for the small number of homes now connected.
Residuals in the newest phase improve for a day after its hydrants are flushed, then fade again.
Water use per home in the newest phase is the same as in older phases.
The newest phase is the farthest from the plant and its water is the oldest in the system.
Bacteriological samples in the newest phase remain absent for coliform, but residuals sit near 0.1 mg/L.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Low demand in oversized new mains makes the water very old by the time it reaches the newest homes, so the residual decays before arrival.
The newest phase pipes are made of a material that consumes chlorine rapidly.
The plant sends lower residual water to the newest phase on purpose.
Homeowners in the newest phase are removing chlorine with whole house filters.

inference.explanation: Oversized mains with few users mean slow movement and old water, flushing helps only briefly, and per home use is normal. The plant sends one water to everyone, and pipe material or home filters would not explain why flushing the mains themselves restores residual for a day.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Measure residuals and estimate water age at the ends of the newest phase before flushing, right after, and daily for a week.
Cut a coupon from a newest phase main to test its chlorine demand in the lab.
Compare plant outlet residuals on days serving different phases.
Survey newest phase homes for whole house treatment units.

nextClue.explanation: Tracking residual recovery and fade after flushing, against estimated age, confirms whether detention in the oversized mains is consuming the chlorine.

clueText.nc1: Residual jumps after flushing then fades steadily over four days as the water ages again, confirming water age in the oversized mains as the cause.
clueText.nc2: The pipe coupon shows normal demand for its material, so the pipe is not consuming unusual chlorine.
clueText.nc3: The plant outlet residual is the same every day; one water serves all phases.
clueText.nc4: Only one home has a filter unit, far too few to explain phase wide results.

tasks.prompt: SCADA at a small station shows discharge pressure slowly falling over a month, but a test gauge installed beside the sensor reads steady and the pumps sound unchanged.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario booster station; the pressure sensor is mounted on a small tapping that has not been cleaned in years. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: The test gauge and the sensor agreed when the sensor was installed three years ago.
The sensor tapping is found partly plugged with rust scale when isolated and checked.
Pump curves verified by flow and the test gauge match the original performance.
Operators report no change in system pressures or complaints during the month.
The sensor reading drops in steps after each pump start, then holds.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Scale plugging the sensor tapping is damping and dropping the sensed pressure, so the SCADA trend is an instrument problem, not a system problem.
The pumps are wearing out slowly and losing pressure each week.
A growing leak is pulling system pressure down month by month.
The test gauge is the faulty instrument and SCADA is correct.

inference.explanation: A plugged tapping explains a drifting, step changing sensed pressure while the test gauge, pump performance, and customer experience all stay normal. Real pump wear or a leak would show on the test gauge and in complaints, and two instruments disagreeing with the physical evidence points at the fouled sensor.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Clean the sensor tapping, reinstall, and log sensor against test gauge through several pump cycles.
Run a full pump curve test at three flows.
Do a night flow leak check on the zone.
Send the test gauge for calibration first.

nextClue.explanation: Cleaning the tapping and comparing both instruments through pump cycles shows whether the sensor returns to agreement.

clueText.nc1: After cleaning, the sensor matches the test gauge within 5 kPa through all cycles, confirming the plugged tapping caused the false decline.
clueText.nc2: The pump curve test matches original performance, so the pumps are not wearing.
clueText.nc3: Night flows are at the normal minimum, giving no sign of a growing leak.
clueText.nc4: The test gauge passes calibration, so it was the reliable reading all along.

tasks.prompt: A chlorine booster station partway along a long distribution main shows residuals downstream swinging between 0.2 and 1.1 mg/L over each day, while the incoming residual is steady.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario booster chlorination station using a small diaphragm pump paced by a flow signal; records are for training only.

evidence.label: Downstream swings follow the same pattern each day, worst at low night flows.
The booster pump's stroke counter shows it delivers in bursts, then nothing for long stretches at low flow.
The flow signal to the pump comes from a meter that reads zero below a cutoff flow the station often sits under at night.
Incoming residual and main pressure are steady around the clock.
The chemical tank is full and the pump primes reliably when stroked by hand.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The flow pacing signal drops out at low night flows, so the booster pump stops and starts in bursts and the downstream residual swings with it.
The incoming water residual is swinging and the booster is faithfully following it.
The booster pump diaphragm has ruptured and leaks chemical back to the tank.
Downstream customers use water in a pattern that consumes chlorine unevenly.

inference.explanation: Incoming residual is steady, the pump bursts match the flow signal cutting out at low flow, and the swing pattern repeats daily with the low flow period. A ruptured diaphragm would lose prime and feed poorly at all flows, and customer use cannot create swings this regular.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Log the flow signal, pump strokes, and downstream residual together for 24 hours to line up the dropouts with the residual swings.
Log incoming residual hourly for a day.
Inspect the pump diaphragm and check valves.
Survey downstream water use by hour from meter data.

nextClue.explanation: A combined 24 hour log shows directly whether residual swings line up with flow signal dropouts and pump stoppages.

clueText.nc1: Every residual dip follows a flow signal dropout and a pump stoppage at low night flow, confirming the pacing signal as the cause of the swings.
clueText.nc2: Incoming residual stays within 0.05 mg/L all day, so the booster was not following an incoming swing.
clueText.nc3: The diaphragm and check valves are intact and the pump holds prime.
clueText.nc4: Meter data shows smooth use patterns that do not match the sharp residual swings.

tasks.prompt: A small plant drawing from a reservoir finds its intake flow limited every February, and the problem clears each spring without any work being done on the intake pipe.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario reservoir intake set just below the winter ice level in a shallow bay; records are from five winters of logs for training only.

evidence.label: The limitation appears only when ice cover on the bay exceeds about 300 mm thick.
A camera inspection in February shows the intake bell surrounded by anchor ice growth on the bay bottom.
Summer inspections show the bell and screen completely clear.
Raw water pumps test at full capacity against a hydrant each spring.
The bay is the shallowest part of the reservoir and freezes earliest.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Anchor ice growing around the shallow intake bell in the coldest weeks is restricting flow, and it melts away each spring.
The intake pipe is collapsing a little more each winter and healing each spring.
Sediment is burying the intake each winter and washing away each spring.
The reservoir level drops each February below the intake bell.

inference.explanation: Camera evidence of anchor ice on the bell, a shallow early freezing bay, ice thickness tracking the problem, and a clear summer inspection all fit anchor ice. A pipe cannot collapse and heal seasonally, sediment does not vanish each spring, and levels are not reported low.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Lower a camera to the intake during the next February restriction and record the bell condition against ice thickness on the bay.
Excavate and inspect the intake pipe in the summer.
Survey sediment depth around the bell each season.
Log reservoir level against the bell elevation all winter.

nextClue.explanation: Filming the bell during a restriction, alongside ice thickness, confirms anchor ice as the seasonal blockage.

clueText.nc1: The February video shows anchor ice coating the bell and screen while the bay ice is at its thickest, confirming the seasonal ice restriction.
clueText.nc2: The summer pipe inspection shows a sound pipe with no collapse.
clueText.nc3: Sediment depth around the bell is unchanged between seasons.
clueText.nc4: Reservoir level stays well above the bell all winter.

tasks.prompt: A small plant measures chlorine contact time far below the clearwell's theoretical value in a tracer study, even though the tank volume and flow give a comfortable paper detention time.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant with a single rectangular clearwell, inlet and outlet at the same end; records are from the tracer study for training only.

evidence.label: The tracer appears at the outlet within 8 minutes, though theoretical detention is 90 minutes.
Inlet and outlet are both located at the south end of the tank.
There are no baffles inside the clearwell.
Residual at the outlet varies with plant flow more than the volume would suggest.
Temperature layers in the tank show a warm stream running along the surface from inlet to outlet.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Water is short circuiting straight from inlet to outlet along the surface, so much of the clearwell volume is not being used for contact time.
The clearwell is leaking half its volume to ground each day.
The tracer chemical is being destroyed by chlorine before it can be measured.
The flow meter over reads, so the real detention is actually longer.

inference.explanation: Tracer arriving in 8 minutes against a 90 minute theoretical time, inlet and outlet at the same end, no baffles, and a warm surface stream all show short circuiting. A leak would show in level accounting, tracer loss would delay rather than speed its arrival, and a meter error would not create the surface stream.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Run a second tracer study after installing temporary baffle curtains and compare the time for the tracer peak to arrive.
Balance clearwell levels against inflow and outflow for a week to look for leakage.
Test tracer recovery in a bench sample of chlorinated clearwell water.
Verify the flow meter against a timed tank drawdown.

nextClue.explanation: Repeating the tracer study with baffles shows whether guiding the flow lengthens the real contact time as the short circuit explanation predicts.

clueText.nc1: With baffles, the tracer peak arrival stretches from 8 minutes to over 45 minutes, confirming short circuiting and the value of baffling.
clueText.nc2: Level accounting balances within normal measurement error, so the tank is not leaking.
clueText.nc3: Bench recovery of the tracer in chlorinated water is near complete, so chlorine was not destroying it.
clueText.nc4: The flow meter verifies within 2 percent on the drawdown test.

tasks.prompt: When a small system's two wells run together on high demand days, total output is much less than the sum of each well pumping alone, and levels in both wells fall sharply.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario well field with two wells 40 m apart in the same sand aquifer; records are from the demand day log for training only.

evidence.label: Well 1 alone gives 12 L/s and Well 2 alone gives 11 L/s, but together they give only 16 L/s.
Pumping levels in both wells drop several extra metres when both run.
Each well recovers fully overnight when the other is off.
Both pumps test at their rated curves when run one at a time.
The wells are screened in the same aquifer unit at the same depth.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The wells interfere with each other: their cones of depression overlap, so each well's drawdown adds to the other's and total yield falls.
Both pumps are failing at the same time on high demand days.
The aquifer cannot supply more than 16 L/s in total to any wells.
The discharge header is too small and throttles both pumps together.

inference.explanation: Combined yield well below the sum of singles, extra drawdown in both wells only when both run, full recovery overnight, and pumps that test fine individually all fit overlapping cones of depression. A hard aquifer limit would not let each well produce its full rate alone on other days, and a header limit would not deepen well drawdown.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Run a pumping test with one well pumping and an observation log of the other well's level to measure the interference drawdown.
Test each pump's curve separately against a flow meter.
Run a long aquifer test with a single well at maximum rate.
Measure pressures along the discharge header with both pumps running.

nextClue.explanation: Pumping one well while watching the other's level measures exactly how much drawdown the wells impose on each other.

clueText.nc1: The idle well's level falls 2.5 m when its neighbour pumps, confirming interference between the overlapping cones of depression.
clueText.nc2: Each pump meets its rated curve when tested alone.
clueText.nc3: A single well sustains its full rate for 24 hours, so the aquifer can supply more than the combined figure suggests.
clueText.nc4: Header pressures stay within design with both pumps running.

tasks.prompt: A well that normally produces clear water turns reddish after the operator raises the pumping rate to meet summer demand, and iron in the discharge climbs with the rate.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario well near the edge of an iron rich clay layer; records are from the summer log for training only.

evidence.label: At the winter rate of 8 L/s the water is clear with iron at 0.1 mg/L.
At the summer rate of 14 L/s, iron rises to 1.8 mg/L and the water turns orange after aeration.
Drawdown at the higher rate pulls the pumping level down near the top of the clay layer shown on the well log.
Iron falls back within a day whenever the rate is reduced.
Neighbouring wells at steady rates show no iron change this summer.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The higher rate's extra drawdown is pulling iron rich water from the clay layer into the well, and lowering the rate keeps that water out.
The well casing has rusted through and is shedding iron at high flow.
The iron is coming from the distribution pipes, not the well.
Summer heat is dissolving iron from the aquifer sand itself.

inference.explanation: Iron that rises and falls with pumping rate, drawdown reaching the clay layer at the high rate, and quick recovery at lower rate all point to rate driven capture of iron rich water. Casing rust would not switch off within a day of a rate cut, and distribution iron cannot appear in a discharge sample at the wellhead.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Step the pumping rate up in stages, sampling iron and logging drawdown at each step to find the rate where iron begins to climb.
Run a camera survey of the casing looking for rust through holes.
Sample iron at the first customer tap and at the wellhead on the same day.
Log aquifer temperature beside the well through the summer.

nextClue.explanation: A step rate test with iron samples shows the exact pumping rate and drawdown where iron rich water starts entering the well.

clueText.nc1: Iron stays low until drawdown reaches the clay layer, then climbs steeply, confirming the high rate is capturing iron rich water from that layer.
clueText.nc2: The casing is sound on camera with no rust through found.
clueText.nc3: Wellhead iron matches the first tap on the high rate day, so the iron starts at the well.
clueText.nc4: Aquifer temperature barely changes between seasons at that depth.

tasks.prompt: Routine sampling at a small plant that feeds fluoride shows results drifting low over a month, and the operator suspects the feed system before suspecting the lab.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant feeding fluoride to a target near the provincially recommended level; records are from the sampling log for training only.

evidence.label: The fluoride feed pump's day tank level is falling at only half its usual rate.
A calibration column drawdown test shows the pump delivering half its set rate.
The pump's suction strainer is found coated with a white crystalline deposit.
Distribution fluoride results match the plant outlet results, both drifting low together.
The laboratory's quality control samples all pass during the month.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The fluoride feed pump is underdelivering because its suction strainer is fouled with crystalline deposit, so less chemical reaches the water.
The laboratory method is drifting and the plant results are actually on target.
The raw water fluoride has risen and is confusing the results.
Customers' home softeners are removing fluoride before the sampling taps.

inference.explanation: A calibration test proving half delivery, a day tank falling at half rate, and a visibly fouled suction strainer explain the low results directly. Lab quality control passes, and plant outlet samples taken before any home plumbing are low too, ruling out lab drift and home softeners.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Clean the suction strainer, repeat the calibration drawdown test, and resample the plant outlet the next day.
Send split samples to a second laboratory for comparison.
Sample raw water fluoride at the wellhead.
Sample distribution sites before any home treatment units.

nextClue.explanation: Cleaning the strainer and retesting delivery plus the outlet sample confirms whether the fouled suction was starving the feed.

clueText.nc1: After cleaning, the pump delivers its full set rate and the outlet fluoride returns to target, confirming the fouled suction strainer.
clueText.nc2: The second laboratory agrees with the low results from before the cleaning.
clueText.nc3: Raw water fluoride is near zero, as usual for this supply.
clueText.nc4: Samples taken at hydrant flush points were also low, so home units were never the explanation.

tasks.prompt: A ground storage tank at a small plant develops a surface layer of warm water each summer, and samples from its outlet on hot afternoons show lower chlorine and higher heterotrophic counts than morning samples.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant with a large ground tank filled and drawn from the same single pipe at its base; records are for training only.

evidence.label: The tank is filled and drawn through one common pipe at the bottom.
Temperature probes show the top of the tank 6 degrees C warmer than the bottom on hot afternoons.
Outlet chlorine is lowest on hot afternoons after the tank has sat in the sun.
Heterotrophic counts are highest in samples drawn from the tank's top hatch.
In winter, with the tank well mixed by cold inflow, the pattern disappears.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The tank is thermally stratifying in summer, so warm surface water ages without mixing, losing chlorine and growing bacteria while the single inlet outlet pipe short circuits the bottom water.
The tank roof vents are letting contaminated rainwater into the stored water.
The chlorine feed at the plant is failing every afternoon.
The tank lining is leaching nutrients that feed bacteria in summer.

inference.explanation: Measured temperature layering, worst quality in the warm top layer, a single bottom pipe that lets new water bypass the top, and the pattern vanishing in winter all fit stratification and stagnation. Rain ingress would not follow temperature layers, and plant feed failure would affect the whole day, not just hot afternoons.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Sample chlorine and temperature at three depths in the tank on a hot afternoon, and repeat after running a tank mixer trial or a fill and draw cycle.
Inspect the roof vents and hatches for gaps after a rain.
Log plant chlorine feed rate and outlet residual hourly for a day.
Take lining coupon samples for a leaching test.

nextClue.explanation: Depth sampling on a hot afternoon maps the warm, low chlorine layer, and a mixing trial shows whether breaking stratification restores quality.

clueText.nc1: The top layer is warm with chlorine near 0.1 mg/L while the bottom is cool at 0.8 mg/L, and after mixing the whole tank reads evenly, confirming summer stratification.
