clueText.nc2: Vents and hatches are screened and sealed, with no sign of rain entry.
clueText.nc3: Plant feed and outlet residual are steady all day, so afternoons are not a feed problem.
clueText.nc4: The lining coupon test is clean, giving no nutrient leaching.

tasks.prompt: During a watermain break on a side street, several homes two streets away report brown water and one reports water briefly flowing backward from a basement tap when the break was isolated.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario distribution system; the break drained a small pressure district for about an hour. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: System pressure in the district fell to near zero while the break ran free.
The backward flow report came while crews were closing valves around the break.
Brown water reports cluster around the break area and fade after flushing.
Bacteriological samples taken after flushing and repressurization are all absent for coliform.
The break was a longitudinal split in an old cast iron main.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The break dropped district pressure to near zero, stirring sediment and creating conditions where backflow could occur at unprotected connections while the main was depressurized.
The plant sent contaminated water into the district during the repair.
The brown water is from a sewage main that broke at the same time.
The backward flow report proves the treatment plant pumps ran in reverse.

inference.explanation: Near zero pressure during the break, sediment stirred by the high velocities, and backflow risk at unprotected taps during depressurization explain every report. The plant's water tested clean, no sewage break was found, and plant pumps cannot run a district backward through a break event.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Collect bacteriological samples at the break area after flushing, and survey the affected homes for backflow protection on basement and hose connections.
Sample the plant treated water hourly during the next repair event.
Excavate the parallel sewer to check for a simultaneous break.
Test the plant high lift pumps for reverse rotation.

nextClue.explanation: Clean post repair samples plus a backflow survey show whether the risk was depressurization at unprotected connections, as the evidence suggests.

clueText.nc1: All post flush samples are absent for coliform, and two homes near the break are found with unprotected basement connections, confirming the depressurization and backflow risk picture.
clueText.nc2: Plant treated water stays fully compliant through the event records.
clueText.nc3: The parallel sewer is intact when checked by camera.
clueText.nc4: The high lift pumps test normally and cannot run in reverse.

tasks.prompt: Operators at a small plant notice a strong chlorine smell in the chemical room each morning, strongest near the hypochlorite totes, though no liquid spill is visible.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant chemical room with bulk hypochlorite totes and a muriatic acid drum stored for pH adjustment; records are for training only.

evidence.label: The smell is strongest first thing in the morning after the room has been closed all night.
A hypochlorite tote's vent cap is found dripping, and a small dried chemical trail runs toward a floor drain.
The muriatic acid drum is stored on the same containment pallet as the hypochlorite tote.
The room exhaust fan is on a timer that shuts it off overnight.
Gas detector readings peak at the floor drain, where the two chemical trails can mix.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Hypochlorite leaking slowly from the tote vent is reaching acid residue at the shared drain, releasing chlorine gas that builds up overnight with the exhaust fan off.
The hypochlorite totes are simply old and the smell is normal off gassing.
The gas detector is faulty and there is no chlorine in the air.
A chlorine gas cylinder in the room is leaking at its valve.

inference.explanation: A dripping tote, chemical trails converging at a drain, acid and hypochlorite stored together, detector peaks at that drain, and overnight buildup with the fan off all point to the two chemicals mixing and releasing chlorine gas. Normal off gassing would not peak at the drain, and this plant stores no gas cylinders.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Separate the acid and hypochlorite storage, repair the tote vent, run the exhaust continuously, and log detector readings at the drain over several nights.
Replace both hypochlorite totes with fresh stock.
Replace the gas detector with a new unit.
Search the room for a leaking gas cylinder valve.

nextClue.explanation: Separating the chemicals, fixing the leak, and ventilating continuously, then logging the drain readings, tests the mixing explanation directly.

clueText.nc1: Detector readings at the drain fall to zero and stay there after separation and repairs, confirming chlorine gas was forming where the leaked chemicals mixed.
clueText.nc2: The original totes, once vented and separated, give no further readings, so age alone was not the cause.
clueText.nc3: The original detector reads correctly on a test gas, so it was not faulty.
clueText.nc4: There are no gas cylinders anywhere in this plant's inventory.

tasks.prompt: At a small sewage lift station, the wet well fills three times faster than normal during a spring rain, and both pumps run almost continuously while the rain lasts.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario collection system serving a village with older clay sewers; records are from the station log for training only.

evidence.label: Wet well inflow tracks rainfall closely, rising within an hour of rain starting and falling a few hours after it stops.
The extra inflow looks clear in the wet well sight glass, not like normal sewage.
Dry weather flows at the station are normal for the season.
Upstream manholes show surcharged levels during the rain that settle afterward.
No new homes or industries connected to the system this year.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Rain derived inflow and infiltration is entering the older sewers through cracks, joints, and connections, overwhelming the station during storms.
Both lift pumps have lost capacity and can no longer keep up with normal flow.
A factory has begun discharging its process water to the sewer.
The wet well level floats are set wrong and the well only looks fuller.

inference.explanation: Flow that tracks rainfall with an hour's lag, clear looking extra water, normal dry weather flow, and surcharging upstream all fit rain derived inflow and infiltration. Pump capacity loss would show in dry weather too, and no new discharger exists.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Log station inflow against a rain gauge for the next three storms, and inspect upstream manholes during rain for clear water entering at joints.
Time each pump's drawdown rate in dry weather to check capacity.
Sample the inflow for industrial chemicals during the next storm.
Raise the float settings and observe the well for a week.

nextClue.explanation: Matching inflow to rainfall and seeing clear water enter at joints during a storm confirms rain derived inflow and infiltration.

clueText.nc1: Inflow rises and falls with each storm, and clear water is seen jetting in at two manhole joints, confirming rain derived inflow and infiltration.
clueText.nc2: Both pumps draw the well down at their rated rate in dry weather, so capacity is fine.
clueText.nc3: Storm samples look and test like diluted groundwater, not industrial discharge.
clueText.nc4: Float settings were verified correct; the high levels were real inflow.

tasks.prompt: Residents near a lift station complain of rotten egg smells on summer evenings, worst on days when the station has pumped only a few times.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario lift station with a 3 km force main discharging to a gravity sewer near the complaining homes; records are for training only.

evidence.label: The smell is worst at the force main discharge manhole, not at the station itself.
Complaints cluster on hot days when sewage sits longest in the force main between pump runs.
A gas detector at the discharge manhole reads hydrogen sulfide peaks right after each pump run ends.
The force main detention time is about 9 hours at current dry weather flows.
Concrete at the discharge manhole crown is soft and corroding.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Sewage going septic during its long detention in the force main generates hydrogen sulfide, which is released at the discharge manhole and is corroding its crown.
The lift station's vent stack is blowing sewage gas toward the homes.
A dead animal in the gravity sewer is causing the smell.
The residents are smelling a nearby farm's manure spreading, not the sewer.

inference.explanation: The smell centred at the discharge manhole, sulfide peaks tied to pump runs, 9 hour detention in warm weather, and crown corrosion at that manhole all fit septic sewage generating hydrogen sulfide in the force main. The station vent, a dead animal, or farm odours would not produce detector peaks synchronized with pumping or the corrosion pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Log hydrogen sulfide at the discharge manhole alongside pump run times for a week, and inspect the manhole crown condition.
Extend the station vent stack and see if complaints change.
Camera the gravity sewer looking for an obstruction or carcass.
Log wind direction against complaint times to check the farm theory.

nextClue.explanation: Pairing sulfide readings with pump runs over a week shows whether the gas arrives with force main discharge, as the septic sewage explanation predicts.

clueText.nc1: Sulfide peaks arrive with each discharge and are highest after the longest detention periods, confirming septic force main sewage as the source.
clueText.nc2: Complaints continue unchanged after the vent work, so the station vent was not the pathway.
clueText.nc3: The camera run shows a clean sewer with no obstruction or carcass.
clueText.nc4: Complaints occur on calm and windy days alike, with no match to spreading days at the farm.

tasks.prompt: A small activated sludge plant's clarifier blanket is rising and the sludge volume index has climbed from 90 to 240 mL/g over three weeks, with stringy filaments visible under the microscope.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario extended aeration plant; records are from the lab bench sheets for training only.

evidence.label: Settled sludge in the cylinder stays fluffy and occupies most of the volume after 30 minutes.
Microscopy shows abundant filamentous organisms bridging between floc particles.
Aeration basin dissolved oxygen has been running at 0.4 mg/L, below the plant's 2 mg/L target.
Effluent suspended solids are rising as the blanket approaches the weirs.
Food to microorganism ratio has been steady, and no toxic discharges are known.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Filamentous bulking driven by the low dissolved oxygen in the basin is preventing the sludge from compacting and settling.
The clarifier rake has stopped and sludge is piling up mechanically.
The plant is simply producing too much sludge and needs more wasting only.
Denitrification in the clarifier is floating the whole blanket with gas.

inference.explanation: High SVI with fluffy, slow compacting sludge, filaments bridging the floc, and weeks of low basin oxygen fit filamentous bulking selected by low DO. A stopped rake would pile sludge unevenly, extra sludge mass alone would still compact well, and denitrification floats chunks with bubbles rather than raising SVI in the cylinder test.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Raise basin dissolved oxygen to target and track SVI, blanket depth, and microscopy weekly for a month.
Inspect the clarifier rake drive for operation.
Double the wasting rate for a week and watch SVI.
Measure nitrate in the clarifier blanket and look for gas bubbles in the settled cylinder.

nextClue.explanation: Holding DO at target while tracking SVI and filaments shows whether the low oxygen was selecting the filamentous growth.

clueText.nc1: SVI falls steadily toward 120 mL/g and filaments decline as DO is held at target, confirming low DO filamentous bulking.
clueText.nc2: The rake turns normally on inspection, so mechanical piling was not occurring.
clueText.nc3: Extra wasting alone in a past event did not change SVI until oxygen was corrected.
clueText.nc4: The settled cylinder shows no gas bubbles and blanket nitrate is low, so denitrification was not floating the sludge.

tasks.prompt: A small plant's effluent has turned slightly cloudy with tiny specks, and the mixed liquor settles fast but leaves a turbid supernatant full of pinpoint floc.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario activated sludge plant that has been wasting very little sludge this quarter; records are for training only.

evidence.label: The sludge age calculates to about 38 days, well above the plant's usual 15 to 20 days.
Floc under the microscope is very small and compact, with few stalked ciliates and many free bacteria in the water between flocs.
The settle test clears a sharp interface quickly but the liquid above stays cloudy.
Effluent BOD is creeping up along with the cloudiness.
Dissolved oxygen in the basin is high at 4.5 mg/L from constant aeration.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The sludge is too old: an excessive sludge age with over aeration is breaking the floc into pin floc that settles but leaves fine particles behind.
A filamentous bulking event is starting and the sludge will soon stop settling.
A toxic slug has killed the biomass and the cloudiness is dead cells.
The clarifier is hydraulically overloaded and washing solids out.

inference.explanation: Very old sludge, tiny compact floc, fast settling with cloudy supernatant, and rising effluent BOD are the textbook picture of pin floc from excessive sludge age. Bulking would slow settling, a toxic kill would show a sudden change with dead indicators, and hydraulic overload would not shrink the floc under the microscope.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Increase wasting in steps to bring sludge age toward 18 days and track effluent turbidity, floc size, and indicator organisms weekly.
Chlorinate the return sludge to attack filaments.
Reseed the basin with sludge from a neighbouring plant.
Reduce plant flow by holding influent in the equalization tank.

nextClue.explanation: Bringing sludge age down gradually and watching floc size and effluent clarity confirms whether old sludge was producing the pin floc.

clueText.nc1: As sludge age falls toward 20 days, floc grows larger, supernatant clears, and effluent BOD recovers, confirming pin floc from excessive sludge age.
clueText.nc2: There were no filaments to attack; microscopy showed the opposite condition.
clueText.nc3: The existing biomass recovered on its own once wasting increased, so reseeding was unnecessary.
clueText.nc4: Flows were within design all along, so hydraulic overload was not the cause.

tasks.prompt: Dissolved oxygen in a small plant's aeration basin has fallen to 0.3 mg/L by midday even with the blower running at full speed, and effluent ammonia is starting to rise.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant with one duty blower and coarse bubble diffusers; records are from the operations log for training only.

evidence.label: The blower discharge pressure is higher than its normal reading at full speed.
Air flow to the basin, measured at the header, is 30 percent below normal.
The blower's inlet air filter is found matted with dust and pollen.
Influent BOD today is at its normal weekday level.
Basin temperature and mixed liquor concentration are in their normal ranges.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The matted inlet filter is starving the blower of air, so oxygen transfer cannot keep up with a normal load.
A toxic discharge has killed the nitrifying bacteria overnight.
The diffusers have all fouled at once and blocked the air.
The plant received a huge organic load this morning that used up the oxygen.

inference.explanation: High discharge pressure with low delivered air and a visibly matted inlet filter explain the oxygen shortfall mechanically. Influent load is normal, which rules out an overload, and a toxic kill would not raise blower pressure or reduce air flow.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Clean or replace the inlet filter, then log blower pressure, air flow, and basin DO through the next full day.
Sample influent for toxicity indicators and industrial chemicals.
Lift and inspect a diffuser grid for fouling.
Composite sample influent BOD every two hours for a day.

nextClue.explanation: Restoring the air supply and watching pressure, flow, and DO recover is the direct test of the starved blower explanation.

clueText.nc1: With a clean filter, discharge pressure normalizes, air flow returns, and basin DO holds 2 mg/L all day, confirming the matted inlet filter.
clueText.nc2: Influent samples show no toxic indicators, and ammonia removal recovers with the air supply.
clueText.nc3: The lifted diffusers bubble evenly once full air flow is restored.
clueText.nc4: The composite confirms influent BOD stayed at normal levels through the event.

tasks.prompt: Over two months, a small plant's effluent BOD has crept from 8 to 19 mg/L while influent BOD is unchanged, and the operator notes mixed liquor suspended solids have fallen by a third.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario activated sludge plant; a new operator increased wasting in the spring to control the blanket and kept the higher rate. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: MLSS has fallen from 2,400 to 1,600 mg/L since the wasting rate was raised.
Food to microorganism ratio has risen as the biomass inventory fell.
Effluent ammonia is still fully nitrified and low.
Settleability is good and the clarifier blanket is thin.
No new industries have connected, and influent BOD and flow are at their usual values.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The plant has wasted away too much of its biomass, so the remaining microorganisms are overloaded and BOD removal has slipped.
A slow toxic leak into the sewer is poisoning the biomass a little more each week.
The clarifier is losing solids that are being counted as BOD in the effluent.
The influent has secretly become much stronger than the lab results show.

inference.explanation: Falling MLSS after a wasting increase, a rising food to microorganism ratio, good settling with a thin blanket, and unchanged influent all point to too little biomass for the load. A toxic effect would usually hit nitrification first, but ammonia is still low, and clarifier solids loss would show in effluent suspended solids and the blanket.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Reduce wasting in steps to rebuild MLSS toward 2,400 mg/L and track effluent BOD and the food to microorganism ratio weekly.
Run a toxicity scan on influent samples for a month.
Track effluent suspended solids against effluent BOD daily.
Composite the influent with a second sampler for comparison.

nextClue.explanation: Rebuilding the biomass inventory and watching BOD removal recover confirms whether over wasting caused the decline.

clueText.nc1: As MLSS rebuilds, effluent BOD falls back below 10 mg/L at the same influent load, confirming the plant had wasted away too much biomass.
clueText.nc2: The toxicity scan finds nothing above background in the influent.
clueText.nc3: Effluent suspended solids stayed low throughout, so solids loss was not inflating the BOD.
clueText.nc4: The second sampler agrees with the plant's influent results.

tasks.prompt: A small plant's manually cleaned grit channel is blinding over with grit and rags within a day of cleaning, and headworks flooding threatens during peak flows.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant with a constant velocity grit channel; a new subdivision's construction sewers were connected this spring. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: The channel fills with a mix of grit, sand, and construction debris, not normal sewage grit alone.
Flow velocity through the channel measures well below the design 0.3 m/s at average flow.
Upstream, construction site runoff has been entering open manholes near the new subdivision.
The bar screen ahead of the channel is intact and catching rags normally.
Peak hour flows have not increased this year.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Low channel velocity is letting grit drop out along the whole channel instead of at the collection point, and construction debris is adding to the load faster than manual cleaning can keep up.
The bar screen has a broken bar and is passing everything to the channel.
The grit channel has collapsed and narrowed, trapping material.
Plant flows have doubled, overwhelming the channel's capacity.

inference.explanation: Velocity below the design value explains grit depositing everywhere instead of staying suspended to the hopper, and the construction debris in the mix explains the faster blinding. The screen is intact, flows are unchanged, and a collapse would show as a local blockage, not even deposition.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Measure channel velocity at several flows and inspect the channel profile, then check upstream manholes near the construction area during rain.
Remove and inspect the bar screen bars for damage.
Camera the channel looking for a collapsed section.
Compare this year's flow records with last year's.

nextClue.explanation: Velocity measurements and the upstream inspection confirm whether slow flow and construction debris are overloading the channel.

clueText.nc1: Velocity is low across the day and a construction area manhole is found open with sand washing in, confirming both halves of the explanation.
clueText.nc2: The screen bars are all intact and evenly spaced.
clueText.nc3: The camera shows a sound channel with even deposition, not a collapse.
clueText.nc4: Flow records match last year within a few percent.

tasks.prompt: On warm afternoons, a small plant's secondary clarifier develops rising sludge chunks that pop to the surface with bubbles, while the morning blanket behaves normally.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario nitrifying activated sludge plant; records are from the summer log for training only.

evidence.label: Rising chunks appear after the blanket has sat in the clarifier for several hours.
Gas bubbles are visible inside the rising sludge chunks.
Nitrate in the clarifier effluent is high at 18 mg/L as N, showing full nitrification upstream.
Dissolved oxygen in the return sludge line is near zero.
Increasing the return sludge rate for a day keeps the blanket lower and the rising chunks mostly disappear.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Denitrification in the settled blanket is producing nitrogen gas that floats sludge chunks once the blanket sits too long in the warm clarifier.
Filamentous bulking is making the sludge too light to stay settled.
The scum baffles have failed and surface scum is being mistaken for sludge.
Grease from the influent is floating the sludge to the surface.

inference.explanation: Warm afternoons, a blanket that sits for hours, gas bubbles inside the chunks, high nitrate with no oxygen in the blanket, and relief from faster return pumping are the classic denitrification picture. Bulking would show in settle tests all day, and scum or grease would not contain gas bubbles or respond to return rate.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Track blanket depth, nitrate, and rising chunk frequency while holding a higher return rate for a week.
Run settle tests and microscopy to check for bulking filaments.
Inspect the scum baffle and skimmer operation.
Sample the influent for grease content.

nextClue.explanation: Holding the blanket shallow with a higher return rate while tracking nitrate and chunk frequency confirms denitrification in the blanket.

clueText.nc1: With the blanket kept shallow, rising chunks nearly stop despite the same high nitrate, confirming denitrification in the deep, old blanket.
clueText.nc2: Settle tests and microscopy show normal compaction and few filaments.
clueText.nc3: The baffle and skimmer are working and the material is sludge, not scum.
clueText.nc4: Influent grease is at its usual low level.

tasks.prompt: A small nitrifying plant's effluent pH has slid from 7.1 to 6.3 over a month, ammonia removal is faltering, and the operator has not changed any chemical feeds because the plant feeds none.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant on soft, low alkalinity sewage; records are from the lab log for training only.

evidence.label: Effluent alkalinity measures only 35 mg/L as CaCO3, down from 110 mg/L.
The plant nitrifies about 25 mg/L of ammonia nitrogen on a typical day.
Influent alkalinity is naturally low at 130 mg/L as CaCO3 in this soft water area.
Ammonia in the effluent rises on the days pH is lowest.
No industrial dischargers with acidic waste are connected to the system.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Nitrification is consuming the sewage's limited alkalinity faster than it is replenished, dropping pH and beginning to inhibit the nitrifiers themselves.
An acidic industrial discharge is secretly entering the sewer at night.
The pH probe has drifted and the plant chemistry is actually normal.
The influent has become septic and is arriving as acid.

inference.explanation: Nitrification consumes about 7.1 mg of alkalinity for every milligram of ammonia nitrogen oxidized, so nitrifying 25 mg/L against a low natural alkalinity explains the steady alkalinity and pH slide and the faltering ammonia removal. Grab samples confirm the probe, and there is no industrial source on the system.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Measure alkalinity and ammonia in and out daily for two weeks to build the consumption balance, and verify pH with bench grab samples.
Sample the sewer at night looking for an acidic discharge slug.
Recalibrate the pH probe and compare with a second meter.
Measure influent pH and sulfide hourly for a day to check for septic inflow.

nextClue.explanation: An alkalinity balance across the plant shows whether nitrification consumption matches the observed loss.

clueText.nc1: Alkalinity consumption matches the nitrification demand almost exactly, and bench pH agrees with the probe, confirming alkalinity consumption by nitrification.
clueText.nc2: Night samples show normal pH and no acid slugs entering the plant.
clueText.nc3: The second meter agrees with the probe within 0.05 pH units.
clueText.nc4: Influent arrives at normal pH with low sulfide, so it is not septic acid inflow.

tasks.prompt: During an intense summer thunderstorm, a dozen homes on one low street report sewage backing up into basements, while the treatment plant itself handles the storm without bypassing.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario town with combined sewers in the older low lying area near the river; records are from the storm log for training only.

evidence.label: Backups happen only during the heaviest rain bursts and stop soon after rain eases.
The street's combined sewer manhole is surcharged to within 0.5 m of the surface during the storm.
Homes that had backwater valves installed report no backups.
The river level is high and the storm outfall is partly submerged.
Dry weather inspections show the street's sewer is clean and in good condition.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Storm flow in the combined sewer, worsened by the submerged outfall, surcharges the pipe and pushes sewage back through unprotected home connections on the low street.
The street's sewer has collapsed and cannot pass even storm flow.
The treatment plant refused the flow and pushed sewage back up the street.
Each home's own lateral is blocked with roots at the same time.

inference.explanation: Backups timed to peak rain, a surcharged manhole, protected homes staying dry, a submerged outfall raising tailwater, and a clean bill of health for the pipe in dry weather all fit storm surcharge. A collapse would misbehave in dry weather too, and a dozen laterals do not block simultaneously.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Log manhole levels on the street against rainfall during the next major storm and survey which homes lack backwater valves.
Camera the street sewer in dry weather looking for collapse.
Review plant influent records for the storm period.
Rod the lateral of one affected home.

nextClue.explanation: Level logging against rainfall shows whether the sewer surcharges exactly when backups occur.

clueText.nc1: Manhole levels peak with the rain bursts and with each backup call, and every backed up home lacks a backwater valve, confirming storm surcharge as the cause.
clueText.nc2: The camera shows a clean, sound sewer barrel.
clueText.nc3: Plant records show it accepted the full storm flow without bypass.
clueText.nc4: The rodded lateral is clear, so the blockage was not in the home's pipe.

tasks.prompt: A gravity sewer behind a row of restaurants needs jetting every six weeks for the same greasy blockage, while other streets on the same route stay clear for years.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario collection system; three restaurants and a bakery discharge to this sewer reach. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: The jetting returns are full of white and yellow greasy chunks that smell of food oil.
The blockage always forms at the same flatter section of pipe.
Two of the three restaurants have no grease interceptor records on file.
Residential streets upstream and downstream of the restaurant row are clear.
The problem worsens in winter when the grease is firmer in the cold pipe.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Fats, oils, and grease from the restaurant discharges are congealing at the flat section and rebuilding the blockage after every jetting.
Tree roots are growing into the pipe and catching sewage solids.
The pipe has a sag that is filling with grit and sand.
Construction debris was left in the pipe when the street was built.

inference.explanation: Greasy food smelling returns, the restaurant row location, missing interceptor records, clear residential reaches, and worse behaviour in cold weather all point to fats, oils, and grease. Roots would come back as fibrous masses, a sag would collect grit, and construction debris would not rebuild every six weeks.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Camera the reach right after jetting and again in four weeks to watch what the new deposit is made of, and audit the restaurants' grease interceptors.
Cut roots from the pipe with a chain flail and camera again.
Run a level survey of the pipe to look for a sag.
Flush the reach with a large water release and watch the downstream manhole.

nextClue.explanation: Watching the deposit rebuild on camera and auditing the interceptors confirms whether restaurant grease is the recurring source.

clueText.nc1: The new deposit is soft grease building from the crown down, and two restaurants are found with missing or undersized interceptors, confirming the grease source.
clueText.nc2: No root masses are seen anywhere in the reach.
clueText.nc3: The level survey shows the design grade with no sag.
clueText.nc4: The flush moves loose material but the greasy crown deposit remains, matching a congealed grease build up.

tasks.prompt: One residential sewer reach blocks about every eight months, and each jetting pulls back fibrous masses; the street is lined with mature maple trees.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario collection system with older clay pipe on a tree lined street; records are for training only.

evidence.label: Jetting returns contain dense fibrous root masses, not grease or grit.
A camera survey shows fine roots entering at several clay pipe joints.
The blockages recur at the same joints after each cutting.
Flow in the reach is normal between blockage events.
The maples' root zones overlap the sewer alignment along the whole street.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Tree roots are entering through the clay pipe joints and regrowing after each cutting, gradually catching solids until the reach blocks.
Grease from homes is building up at the joints.
The pipe joints have offset and are catching solids on the ledges.
Wipes flushed by residents are snagging at one rough spot.

inference.explanation: Fibrous root masses in the returns, roots seen entering at joints on camera, recurrence at those same joints, and the tree lined alignment all fit root intrusion. Grease would look and smell different, offsets would not regrow after cutting, and wipes would not produce root fibres.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Schedule a camera survey six months after root cutting to measure regrowth at the joints, and log blockage dates against the cutting dates.
Sample the blockage material for grease content.
Measure joint offsets with the camera's inclinometer.
Distribute a wipes education flyer and watch blockage frequency.

nextClue.explanation: Regrowth measured at the joints on a timed camera survey confirms roots as the recurring cause.

clueText.nc1: Fine roots are already re entering the same joints at six months, confirming regrowth as the blockage mechanism.
clueText.nc2: The blockage material is almost entirely root fibre with little grease.
clueText.nc3: Joint offsets are minor and do not catch the solids; the roots do.
clueText.nc4: Blockages continue on the same cycle after the flyer, so wipes were not the driver.

tasks.prompt: A lift station's pumps have gradually lost capacity over a year, run times are up 40 percent, and discharge pressure is lower even though the pumps were rebuilt last spring.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario station with a long force main that rises over a hill midway to the discharge; records are for training only.

evidence.label: The force main profile has a distinct high point at the hill crest.
The air release valve at the crest was found seized shut when finally inspected.
Pump performance tests at the station wet well match the rebuilt pumps' curves when discharging to a test header.
Run time growth has been gradual over about a year.
No new connections have added flow to the station this year.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Air accumulating at the force main high point, with the release valve seized, is choking the pipe's cross section and adding head loss the pumps must work against.
The rebuilt pumps were fitted with the wrong impellers.
The force main is tuberculated shut along its whole length.
A partially closed valve at the discharge is throttling the main.

inference.explanation: A high point with a seized air release, gradual capacity loss over a year, and pumps that test perfectly on a test header point to air binding at the crest. Wrong impellers would have shown up immediately after the rebuild and on the test header, and a throttling valve would not grow worse month by month.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Service the crest air release valve, then log pump run times and discharge pressure for a month to compare against the previous trend.
Pull a pump and compare its impeller with the specification.
Pig or camera a section of force main to check for tuberculation.
Count turns on the discharge gate valve to confirm it is fully open.

nextClue.explanation: Freeing the air release and watching run times recover tests whether trapped air at the crest was choking the main.

clueText.nc1: Run times fall steadily back toward normal over two weeks as air is released, confirming air binding at the high point.
clueText.nc2: The impeller matches the specification exactly.
clueText.nc3: The inspected main section shows only light coating, not heavy tuberculation.
clueText.nc4: The discharge valve is confirmed fully open.

tasks.prompt: One pump at a sewage lift station keeps losing capacity for a few days, then suddenly recovering, and its motor current swings while it runs.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario lift station with two submersible pumps alternating duty; the sewershed includes a large apartment complex. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: When the pump is lifted, stringy fibrous material and wipes are wrapped around the impeller.
After cleaning, the pump returns to full capacity at once.
The ragging returns within weeks each time it is cleaned.
The second pump, with a different impeller style, rags much less often.
Current swings disappear whenever the impeller is clean.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Flushable wipes and fibrous material in the sewage are ragging this pump's impeller, cutting its capacity until the material is cleared or sloughs off.
The pump's bearings are failing intermittently and seizing.
The wet well is vortexing and the pump is drawing air.
The discharge check valve is sticking half shut at random.

inference.explanation: Material physically wrapped on the impeller, instant recovery after cleaning, regular recurrence, and current swings that vanish when clean all prove ragging. Bearing failure would not recover with cleaning, vortexing depends on level rather than weeks of operation, and a sticking valve would not put fibres on the impeller.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Log pump capacity weekly and photograph the impeller at each lifting for two months to tie capacity loss to rag build up.
Measure bearing play and temperature on the pump motor.
Watch the wet well surface for vortexing at low levels.
Exercise and inspect the check valve through full travel.

nextClue.explanation: Capacity logs matched with impeller photos show whether rag build up is what erodes performance between cleanings.

clueText.nc1: Capacity falls steadily as rag mass on the impeller grows, and resets with every cleaning, confirming wipes ragging as the cause.
clueText.nc2: Bearings measure within tolerance and run cool.
clueText.nc3: No vortex forms at the operating levels used.
clueText.nc4: The check valve travels fully and seats cleanly.

tasks.prompt: A small plant's aeration basin dissolved oxygen crashes every few weeks on no set schedule, and on those days the influent arrives darker and stronger smelling than usual.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant that accepts hauled septage at a receiving manhole by appointment; records are from the operator log for training only.

evidence.label: DO crashes coincide with days the septage hauler discharged two loads back to back.
A sample taken during one crash shows influent BOD three times the normal value.
The crashes resolve within a day as the slug passes through the plant.
Town sewer flows and strengths are steady on crash days.
The hauler's log shows the crashed days were its largest volume days of the month.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Concentrated septage loads discharged in a short window are shocking the basin with more oxygen demand than the aeration can supply.
The blower is failing intermittently on a random schedule.
Industrial waste is entering the town sewer on the crash days.
The DO probe fouls on those days and the basin is actually fine.

inference.explanation: Crashes tied to double septage loads, a measured triple strength influent sample, one day recovery as the slug passes, and steady town sewage all point to the septage shock load. A failing blower would not match the hauler's schedule, and the probe theory fails because the strong influent sample was measured in the lab.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Log septage receiving times and volumes against basin DO and influent BOD for the next five deliveries.
Log blower run hours and discharge pressure continuously for a month.
Sample town trunk sewers on the next crash day.
Clean and calibrate the DO probe and compare with a portable meter.

nextClue.explanation: Matching delivery records to DO and influent strength shows whether the septage timing drives the crashes.

clueText.nc1: Every DO dip follows a large septage discharge by under an hour, and influent BOD spikes with it, confirming the septage shock load.
clueText.nc2: The blower runs steadily through crash and normal days alike.
clueText.nc3: Trunk sewer samples are at normal strength on crash days.
clueText.nc4: The portable meter agrees with the probe during a crash, so the low DO is real.

tasks.prompt: A small plant's final effluent suspended solids spike every sunny afternoon but are low each morning, and the clarifier launders have a thick green coating.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant with a shallow secondary clarifier exposed to full sun; records are from the summer log for training only.

evidence.label: Effluent TSS rises through the day and falls again overnight.
Green algae mats coat the launders and weirs and pieces slough off into the effluent channel.
Settle tests and blanket depth are normal and steady all day.
Effluent samples taken before the launders, from the clarifier surface centre, are low in solids all day.
The pattern is worst in the sunniest weeks of summer.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Algae growing on the sunny launders and weirs is sloughing into the effluent and causing the afternoon TSS spikes, while the clarifier itself is settling well.
The sludge is bulking every afternoon and recovering every night.
Denitrification floats sludge only during the day.
The sun is interfering with the effluent turbidity meter each afternoon.

inference.explanation: Centre samples staying low while final effluent spikes, visible algae mats sloughing off the launders, normal settle tests, and a sunny season pattern all show the solids are added at the launders, not from settling failure. Bulking or denitrification would raise the centre samples too.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Brush the launders and weirs clean, then log effluent TSS morning and afternoon for two weeks.
Run afternoon settle tests and microscopy during a spike.
Track blanket depth and nitrate through a spike afternoon.
Shade the turbidity meter and compare readings.

nextClue.explanation: Cleaning the launders and watching the afternoon spikes tests whether algae sloughing was adding the solids.

clueText.nc1: Afternoon TSS spikes disappear for the two weeks after brushing and return as the coating regrows, confirming algae on the launders as the source.
clueText.nc2: Afternoon settle tests stay normal during the original spikes.
clueText.nc3: Blanket depth and nitrate are steady through spike afternoons, ruling out floating sludge.
clueText.nc4: The meter reads the same shaded or not; the lab TSS results match it.

tasks.prompt: Each winter, a small plant's effluent ammonia climbs for six to eight weeks even though aeration is unchanged, and it recovers every spring without any equipment repairs.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario extended aeration plant; records are from four winters of lab results for training only.

evidence.label: Effluent ammonia rises as mixed liquor temperature falls below 8 degrees C.
Dissolved oxygen is held at 2 mg/L all winter.
The plant's sludge age is about 12 days, set for summer conditions.
Nitrifier growth rates roughly halve for each 8 to 10 degree drop in temperature.
Effluent BOD stays low all winter, so carbon removal is not failing.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Cold temperatures slow the nitrifiers so much that the summer sludge age washes them out faster than they can grow, and ammonia removal fails until spring.
The blowers lose capacity in cold air every winter.
A winter industrial discharge is poisoning the nitrifiers.
The ammonia analyzer reads falsely high in cold weather.

inference.explanation: Ammonia failure that tracks temperature, adequate oxygen, a sludge age too short for cold nitrifier growth, and BOD removal continuing all fit nitrifier washout in the cold. Blower or poison problems would hurt BOD removal or oxygen too, and lab results confirm the analyzer.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Raise the sludge age before winter by reducing wasting, and track effluent ammonia against mixed liquor temperature through the season.
Test blower output on the coldest days.
Run an influent toxicity screen in mid winter.
Send split effluent samples to a second lab in January.

nextClue.explanation: Lengthening sludge age ahead of the cold and watching ammonia against temperature tests the washout explanation directly.

clueText.nc1: With sludge age raised to 22 days, effluent ammonia stays low through the coldest weeks, confirming cold weather nitrifier washout at the old sludge age.
clueText.nc2: Blower output meets its rating on the coldest test day.
clueText.nc3: The winter toxicity screen is clean.
clueText.nc4: The second lab agrees with the plant's January ammonia results.

tasks.prompt: A small plant develops a thick, dark brown, greasy foam that covers the aeration basin and does not break up with spray water, and it has been building for two months.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario activated sludge plant running a long sludge age for nitrification; records are for training only.

evidence.label: The foam is dark brown, viscous, and stable, and it carries solids onto the walkway.
Microscopy shows branching filamentous organisms of the Nocardia type within the floc.
Sludge age is about 30 days and the plant wastes conservatively.
Effluent quality is still good, but foam traps solids that wash over the clarifier on windy days.
White soapy foam from a detergent discharge is not present; this foam is brown and greasy.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Nocardia type filaments, favoured by the long sludge age and greasy substrates, are stabilizing the brown foam on the basin.
A detergent spill in town is foaming the basin with surfactants.
The plant is in start up and young sludge is making white foam.
Excess air is simply whipping the mixed liquor into a froth.

inference.explanation: Dark brown, greasy, stable foam with branching Nocardia filaments under the microscope and a long sludge age is the classic Nocardia foam picture. Detergent foam is white and breaks up, young sludge foam belongs to start up, and plain air froth collapses quickly and carries no filaments.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Confirm the filament type by microscopy, then trial increased wasting to trim sludge age while tracking foam coverage weekly.
Sample influent for surfactants on foam heavy days.
Check plant records for a recent start up or reseed.
Reduce air flow for a day and watch the foam.

nextClue.explanation: Microscopy plus a wasting trial shows whether trimming sludge age shrinks the Nocardia foam as expected.

clueText.nc1: Foam coverage shrinks steadily as sludge age is trimmed and the branching filaments decline, confirming Nocardia foam tied to the long sludge age.
clueText.nc2: Surfactants in the influent are at normal background levels.
clueText.nc3: The plant has run continuously for years; there was no start up.
clueText.nc4: The foam persists unchanged through the low air day, so it is not simple froth.

tasks.prompt: Two weeks after a small plant restarted a drained aeration basin, the surface carries white, billowy foam and the effluent is cloudy, though loads are normal.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant that reseeded with a tanker of sludge from a neighbouring plant after a maintenance shutdown; records are for training only.

evidence.label: The foam is white, light, and billowy, and breaks down when sprayed.
Mixed liquor suspended solids are still low at 900 mg/L as the new biomass grows.
Microscopy shows dispersed bacteria and few developed flocs or stalked ciliates yet.
The food to microorganism ratio is high because the food is normal but the biomass is small.
Foam and cloudiness lessen a little each week as MLSS climbs.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The young, still growing biomass cannot yet handle the normal load, and the white foam and cloudy effluent are start up conditions that resolve as the sludge matures.
A surfactant discharge from a laundry is foaming the basin.
Nocardia filaments have taken over the basin during the restart.
The clarifier has failed mechanically since the shutdown.

inference.explanation: White billowy foam, low but climbing MLSS, immature microscopy, a high food to microorganism ratio, and steady weekly improvement are the start up picture. A surfactant event would not track biomass growth, Nocardia foam is brown and greasy, and the clarifier cannot explain the basin foam or the immature floc.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Track MLSS, food to microorganism ratio, microscopy, and foam coverage weekly until the sludge matures.
Sample influent for surfactants on the worst foam day.
Stain and identify filaments in the foam under the microscope.
Inspect the clarifier drive and rake.

nextClue.explanation: Weekly tracking as the biomass grows shows whether foam fades in step with sludge maturity, as start up foam should.

clueText.nc1: Foam fades and effluent clears as MLSS reaches normal and stalked ciliates appear, confirming start up young sludge foam.
clueText.nc2: Influent surfactants are unremarkable on the worst day.
clueText.nc3: The foam filaments are not Nocardia; the foam is mostly trapped young floc.
clueText.nc4: The clarifier drive and rake operate normally throughout.

tasks.prompt: A small plant's anaerobic digester gas production has fallen by a third over two weeks, and the operator notes the digester contents feel cooler at the sample tap than usual.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant with a heated anaerobic digester; the boiler circulates hot water through a heat exchanger coil. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: Digester temperature has fallen from 36 to 31 degrees C over two weeks.
Volatile acids are rising and the volatile acid to alkalinity ratio is climbing toward 0.4.
The boiler fires normally but the hot water return from the digester coil is barely warm.
Sludge feed quantity and strength are unchanged.
Scale is visible in the heating coil's strainer when it is opened.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The scaled heating coil is no longer transferring enough heat, so the digester is cooling and its methane producers are slowing down.
A toxic load has killed the methane forming bacteria.
The plant has stopped feeding the digester enough sludge.
The gas meter has failed and production is actually normal.

inference.explanation: Falling temperature, a boiler that fires but returns barely warm water, scale in the coil strainer, and rising volatile acids as the biology cools all fit heat transfer failure. Feed is unchanged, and a toxic kill would not cool the tank or scale the coil.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Clean the heating coil circuit and strainer, then log digester temperature, gas production, and the acid ratio daily for two weeks.
Run a toxicity screen on the digester feed sludge.
Weigh and sample the daily feed sludge for a week.
Test the gas meter against a timed bag fill.

nextClue.explanation: Restoring heat transfer and watching temperature and gas recover confirms the scaled coil as the cause.

clueText.nc1: Temperature climbs back to 36 degrees C and gas production recovers as the acid ratio falls, confirming the scaled heating coil.
clueText.nc2: The feed sludge toxicity screen is clean.
clueText.nc3: Feed quantity and strength match the plant's records all week.
clueText.nc4: The gas meter verifies accurately, so the production drop was real.

tasks.prompt: A small plant's belt press cake has gone from 18 percent solids to a soupy 11 percent over a month, and the press operators are using more wash water than ever to keep the belt clean.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant dewatering anaerobically digested sludge with polymer conditioning; records are for training only.

evidence.label: The polymer dose has not been changed, but the polymer tote was switched to a new supplier's product last month.
Jar tests with the old polymer product give a firm, free draining floc; the new product gives a weak, slimy floc.
Sludge feed solids and flow to the press are unchanged.
Belt condition and tension were checked and are within specification.
Cake quality fell in the same week the polymer product changed.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The replacement polymer product is a poor match for this sludge, so conditioning is weak and the press cannot release water.
The digested sludge itself has changed and can no longer be dewatered.
The press belts have worn out and are blinding.
Operators are feeding the press too fast for it to work.

inference.explanation: Cake quality falling exactly with the polymer change, jar tests showing weak floc with the new product and strong floc with the old, and unchanged sludge and press condition all point to the polymer mismatch. Belt wear or feed rate would not show up in a bench jar test.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Run side by side jar tests and a press trial with the old and new polymers at several doses, measuring cake solids for each.
Send digested sludge samples for a full characterization.
Replace both press belts and rerun the same sludge.
Halve the press feed rate for a full run and measure cake solids.

nextClue.explanation: Press trials comparing the two polymers on the same sludge directly test whether the product change caused the poor cake.

clueText.nc1: The old polymer restores cake to 18 percent solids at the usual dose while the new product stays soupy at every dose, confirming the polymer mismatch.
clueText.nc2: Sludge characterization matches previous years, so the sludge did not change.
clueText.nc3: Cake stays poor on the new belts until the polymer is changed back, ruling out belt wear.
clueText.nc4: Feed rate changes do not fix the cake with the new polymer in place.

tasks.prompt: A small plant disinfecting with UV is failing its effluent E. coli limit on bright weeks, and the UV unit reports it is delivering full intensity.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant with UV disinfection after secondary clarification; records are from the summer log for training only.

evidence.label: Effluent suspended solids are elevated at 28 mg/L, above the plant's usual 10 mg/L.
Algae growth on the clarifier launders sloughs into the effluent on sunny days.
UV transmittance of the effluent has fallen as the solids rose.
Lamp hours and intensity readings are within specification.
E. coli failures line up with the highest solids days, not with lamp output changes.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Suspended solids and algae particles in the effluent are shielding bacteria from the UV light, so disinfection fails even though the lamps are performing.
The UV lamps have lost output and the intensity sensor is lying.
A resistant strain of E. coli has developed in the plant.
The sample bottles are being contaminated at the plant's sampling tap.

inference.explanation: Failures that track solids, falling transmittance, visible algae sloughing, and lamps verified in specification fit particle shielding. Lamp failure would track lamp output, and tap contamination would not follow the solids pattern day by day.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Sample effluent solids, transmittance, and E. coli together daily for two weeks while the launders are kept brushed clean.
Verify lamp output with the reference sensor.
Speciate the E. coli isolates from failed samples.
Take duplicate samples from a second tap for comparison.

nextClue.explanation: Daily paired solids and E. coli results, with the launders kept clean, show whether the failures follow the particles reaching the UV unit.

clueText.nc1: As launder brushing brings effluent solids back near 10 mg/L, transmittance rises and E. coli passes return, confirming particle shielding of the UV light.
clueText.nc2: Lamp output verifies within specification on the reference sensor.
clueText.nc3: The isolates are ordinary E. coli with no unusual resistance.
clueText.nc4: Duplicates from the second tap match the plant tap results.

tasks.prompt: A small plant chlorinating its effluent finds the chlorine residual in the contact tank keeps collapsing, and effluent coliform counts rise on the same days, though the dose has not changed.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant with chlorine disinfection of nitrified effluent; records are from the lab log for training only.

evidence.label: Nitrite in the effluent has risen to 3 mg/L as N on the poor disinfection days.
Ammonia is low, so nitrification is proceeding, but it appears to stall partway.
Chlorine demand tests on the effluent show demand rising in step with nitrite.
Contact tank flows and dose rates are at their normal values.
On days nitrite is low, the same dose holds a good residual and coliforms pass.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Nitrite building up from partial nitrification is exerting a heavy chlorine demand that consumes the dose before it can disinfect.
The chlorine feed pump has lost capacity and is underdosing.
The contact tank has short circuited so water passes in minutes.
The coliform samples are being mishandled and warming up in transit.

inference.explanation: Demand rising in step with nitrite, good performance at the same dose on low nitrite days, and normal flows and feed all point to nitrite demand. A weak pump or short circuit would misbehave every day, not only when nitrite is high.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Measure nitrite, chlorine demand, residual, and coliforms together daily for two weeks and compare high and low nitrite days.
Calibrate the chlorine feed pump output with a drawdown test.
Run a dye trace through the contact tank.
Audit sample transport temperatures with a data logger.

nextClue.explanation: Paired daily measurements show whether disinfection fails exactly when nitrite driven demand is high.

clueText.nc1: Every residual collapse and coliform rise falls on a high nitrite day, and low nitrite days disinfect normally at the same dose, confirming nitrite chlorine demand.
clueText.nc2: The feed pump delivers its set rate on the drawdown test.
clueText.nc3: The dye trace shows the expected contact time through the tank.
clueText.nc4: Sample transport stays within the required temperature range.

tasks.prompt: A concrete trunk sewer manhole near the bottom of a long, flat sewer reach is crumbling at its crown, and crews report strong rotten egg odours whenever they open it.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario collection system; the reach runs nearly flat for 2 km from a small pumping station. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: Corrosion is worst at the manhole crown, above the water line, while the submerged benching is sound.
Hydrogen sulfide readings at the manhole reach 80 ppm on warm mornings.
The sewage arrives warm and septic smelling after its long slow trip down the flat reach.
Sulfide in the sewage is elevated, and the concrete shows the soft, white, pasty surface typical of acid attack.
Manholes on the steeper reaches upstream are in good condition.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Hydrogen sulfide released from the septic sewage is being converted to sulfuric acid on the moist crown, which is eating the concrete above the water line.
Road salt runoff is attacking the manhole from outside.
The manhole was built with defective concrete that is failing on its own.
Tree roots are crushing the manhole structure.

inference.explanation: Crown only corrosion above the water line, high sulfide gas, septic sewage after long flat travel, and acid attacked paste on the crown are the signature of sulfide driven crown corrosion. Sound submerged concrete rules out a general material defect, and the steeper, faster reaches are unaffected because their sewage stays fresher.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Log sulfide gas at the manhole through warm weather and take a small core of crown concrete to test its pH profile.
Sample road runoff near the manhole for salt content.
Test cores from the submerged benching for strength.
Camera the outside of the manhole for root pressure cracks.

nextClue.explanation: A crown core showing acid penetration from the inside surface, matched with high sulfide logs, confirms the crown corrosion mechanism.

clueText.nc1: The crown core is acidic to a depth of 20 mm from the inside face while benching cores are sound, confirming sulfuric acid attack from sewer gas.
clueText.nc2: Runoff salt levels are ordinary and would attack the outside, not the crown interior.
clueText.nc3: Submerged concrete tests at full strength, so the original concrete was not defective.
clueText.nc4: No roots or external cracking are found around the structure.

tasks.prompt: During heavy rain, a small plant's headworks level rises until the bar screen is nearly submerged, and the crew rakes bar loads of material off it through the storm.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant with a manually raked coarse bar screen; the collection system has combined sections. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: The screen blinds fastest during the first hour of heavy rain after a dry week.
Raked material is mostly leaves, sticks, rags, and street litter, not normal sewage solids alone.
Between storms, the screen needs raking only once a day.
Influent flow during the blinding is high but within the screen's rated hydraulic capacity when clean.
Upstream combined sewers carry street runoff directly to the plant.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The first flush of the storm is washing a surge of street debris and litter down the combined sewers that blinds the screen faster than the crew can rake it.
The screen bars have bent and narrowed the openings permanently.
Plant influent pumps downstream are failing and backing water up over the screen.
A single large object is lodged across the screen the whole storm.

inference.explanation: Blinding tied to the first hour of storms after dry weather, debris that is plainly street litter, easy behaviour between storms, and a screen rated for the flow when clean all fit a first flush debris surge. Bent bars or a lodged object would blind the screen in dry weather too, and downstream pumping problems would not fill the screen with street litter.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Log headworks level, rainfall, and raking frequency through the next storm, and photograph the raked material.
Measure bar spacing across the screen for bending.
Check downstream pump run logs during a blinding event.
Camera the screen channel during a storm for a lodged object.

nextClue.explanation: Storm logging with photos of the rakings shows whether the blinding arrives with the first flush debris surge.

clueText.nc1: Level rises and raking peaks in the first storm hour, and the rakings are leaves and litter, confirming the first flush debris surge as the cause.
clueText.nc2: Bar spacing is uniform and matches the specification.
clueText.nc3: Downstream pumps run normally and draw the channel down whenever the screen is raked clear.
clueText.nc4: The camera shows material matting evenly across the bars, not one lodged object.

tasks.prompt: A small plant's primary clarifier gives off strong sewage odours on warm days, and gas bubbles lift black sludge to the surface in patches.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant with one primary clarifier; sludge is withdrawn by a timer the operator set months ago. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: The settled sludge is withdrawn for 10 minutes twice a day, a setting unchanged since winter.
Sludge drawn from the hopper is black and smells strongly of hydrogen sulfide.
Warm weather has raised sewage temperature to 22 degrees C.
Scum and floating sludge patches cover about a third of the surface by afternoon.
When withdrawal is run manually for an hour, the floating patches shrink the next day.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Sludge is sitting in the hopper too long between withdrawals and turning septic, so its gas floats it to the surface and causes the odours.
The clarifier is receiving far more solids than it was designed for.
The rake mechanism has stopped and is not moving sludge to the hopper.
Industrial solvents in the influent are floating the sludge.

inference.explanation: Black sulfide smelling hopper sludge, floating patches with gas, warm sewage speeding septicity, a fixed short withdrawal timer, and improvement after a long manual withdrawal all fit septic sludge from infrequent drawing. An overload would not blacken the hopper sludge this way, and the rake clearly delivers sludge to the hopper since drawing it helps.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Increase withdrawal frequency in steps and log surface coverage, hopper sludge odour, and blanket depth daily for two weeks.
Compare influent solids loading with the clarifier design rating.
Inspect the rake drive for rotation.
Sample influent for solvents on an odour day.

nextClue.explanation: Stepping up withdrawal frequency and watching the surface clear tests whether sludge detention in the hopper was the problem.

clueText.nc1: With withdrawals every few hours, floating patches and odours fade within days, confirming septic sludge from the long hopper detention.
clueText.nc2: Influent loading is at 70 percent of the design rating, so the unit is not overloaded.
clueText.nc3: The rake turns steadily and delivers sludge to the hopper.
clueText.nc4: Solvent results are non detect on the odour day sampled.

tasks.prompt: A small plant's clarifier blanket keeps rising through the day even though the return activated sludge pump is running, and the operator finds the RAS line gurgling at its high point.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant with RAS pumped from the clarifier hopper over a high loop in the return line; records are for training only.

evidence.label: The RAS pump runs but its flow meter reads near zero for long stretches.
Cracking the vent at the line's high point releases a rush of air and flow resumes for a while.
The clarifier blanket rises whenever RAS flow stalls and falls when it runs.
The pump's suction is submerged and the wet well side of the system is normal.
The problem began after the RAS line was drained for a valve repair.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: The return line is air locking at its high point after being drained, so the pump moves air instead of sludge and the blanket builds up.
The RAS pump impeller has worn out and cannot move sludge.
The clarifier rake has failed and sludge cannot reach the hopper.
The plant is making far more sludge than the RAS system was sized for.

inference.explanation: Flow restored by venting air, gurgling at the high point, onset right after the line was drained, and a blanket that tracks RAS flow all prove air locking. A worn impeller would not respond to venting, and the rake and sludge production do not explain air rushing from the vent.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Vent the high point, fit an automatic air release, and log RAS flow and blanket depth together for a week.
Pull the RAS pump and inspect the impeller.
Inspect the clarifier rake operation.
Compare sludge production with the RAS design capacity.

nextClue.explanation: Logging flow and blanket together after venting shows whether keeping air out of the line holds the blanket down.

clueText.nc1: RAS flow stays continuous after the air release is fitted and the blanket holds at its normal depth, confirming air locking at the high point.
clueText.nc2: The impeller is in good condition when checked during planned work.
clueText.nc3: The rake delivers sludge to the hopper normally.
clueText.nc4: Sludge production is well within the return system's capacity.

tasks.prompt: A small plant's rock trickling filter has developed ponding across much of its surface, and the distributor arms have slowed as the ponded areas grow.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario plant with a rock media trickling filter fed by a rotary distributor; records are from the summer log for training only.

evidence.label: Ponded areas hold standing water that does not drain between doses.
Digging into a ponded spot shows the rock voids packed with thick biological growth and fine solids.
Filter flies are abundant and the ponded surface smells sour.
Recirculation rate and distributor speed were verified normal last month.
Effluent BOD from the filter has risen as ponding spread.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Excess biological growth and trapped solids have clogged the rock media voids, so wastewater ponds instead of percolating through the filter.
The distributor arms are bent and dumping all the flow in one area.
The underdrains have collapsed under the media.
The influent has become too strong for any trickling filter to handle.

inference.explanation: Standing water that will not drain, voids physically packed with growth and solids, and performance falling as ponding spreads fit media clogging. The distributor was verified normal, a collapsed underdrain would flood the whole bed from below, and influent strength does not pack voids with solids.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Excavate test pits in ponded and free draining areas and compare void condition, then trial flushing and resting one section.
Level check the distributor arms and measure flow from each nozzle row.
Inspect the underdrain channels at the filter outlet.
Compare influent BOD with the filter's design loading.

nextClue.explanation: Test pits comparing ponded and clear areas show whether clogged voids are what stops the drainage.

clueText.nc1: Ponded pits are packed solid while clear area pits are open, and the rested, flushed section drains again, confirming media clogging by excess growth and solids.
clueText.nc2: The distributor arms are level with even nozzle flow.
clueText.nc3: Underdrain channels run freely at the outlet.
clueText.nc4: Influent loading is within the design range for the filter.

tasks.prompt: A small facultative lagoon system meets its BOD limit but keeps failing its summer effluent suspended solids limit, with the discharge looking green.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario two cell lagoon discharging each spring and summer; records are from the discharge sampling for training only.

evidence.label: Effluent TSS is mostly volatile; the green colour comes from algae cells counted high in the sample.
Effluent BOD passes comfortably on the same samples that fail TSS.
Algae counts in the final cell peak after two weeks of sunny, calm weather.
TSS is lowest in samples drawn early in the morning and highest in mid afternoon.
The first cell is performing normally with no sludge carryover signs.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Algae growing in the sunlit final cell are themselves the suspended solids failing the limit, a seasonal lagoon behaviour rather than a treatment breakdown.
Sludge from the first cell is washing over the intercell structure into the discharge.
The lagoon liner has failed and soil is clouding the effluent.
Short circuiting is sending raw sewage straight to the outlet.

inference.explanation: Volatile, green, algae rich solids that peak with sun and time of day, while BOD passes and the first cell behaves, identify algal solids. Sludge carryover or short circuiting would raise BOD along with TSS, and soil from a liner failure would be inorganic, not green and volatile.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Run effluent samples for total and volatile solids plus algae counts morning and afternoon for a week of discharge.
Inspect the intercell structure for sludge deposits passing over.
Dye test the cells for short circuiting.
Survey the final cell bottom for liner damage.

nextClue.explanation: Splitting the effluent solids into volatile and algae fractions across the day confirms whether algae are the failing solids.

clueText.nc1: Most of the effluent solids are volatile algae that peak in the afternoon sun, confirming algal TSS as the cause of the summer failures.
clueText.nc2: The intercell structure is clean with no sludge passing.
clueText.nc3: The dye travels cell to cell with no shortcut to the outlet.
clueText.nc4: The bottom survey finds the liner intact.

tasks.prompt: A two cell lagoon that used to meet its limits now discharges effluent with BOD nearly as high as its influent on windy weeks, though the cells look unchanged.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario lagoon where a spring flood shifted the inlet pipe; records are from the discharge log for training only.

evidence.label: A dye test reaches the outlet in 2 days against a design detention of 40 days.
The inlet pipe is found displaced so it discharges close to the intercell opening.
Effluent quality is worst when wind blows from the inlet toward the outlet.
Sludge surveys show deep deposits in the far corners that the flow never reaches.
Influent strength and flows are at their normal values.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Flow is short circuiting from the displaced inlet straight through to the outlet, so most of the lagoon volume never treats the wastewater.
The lagoon biomass has died off and stopped treating.
The influent has become far stronger than the lab shows.
The outlet structure is leaking raw sewage from the first cell.

inference.explanation: A 2 day dye arrival against 40 days design, a displaced inlet near the intercell opening, wind driven worsening, and untouched sludge in the far corners all prove short circuiting. Dead biomass would not speed the dye, and the lab influent matches the plant's other checks.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check or sample would best confirm or sharpen this inference?

options.label: Repeat the dye test after the inlet is realigned to discharge at the far end of the first cell, and compare travel time.
Run a full microbial activity test on lagoon samples.
Composite influent with a second sampler.
Inspect and pressure test the outlet structure.

nextClue.explanation: Repeating the dye test after realigning the inlet shows whether the flow path and detention are restored.

clueText.nc1: Dye travel time stretches past three weeks after realignment and effluent BOD falls back within limits, confirming the short circuit.
clueText.nc2: Lagoon samples show active biology once the flow actually reaches them.
clueText.nc3: The second sampler confirms the original influent results.
clueText.nc4: The outlet structure is sound and passes its test.

tasks.prompt: A village's treatment plant receives double its normal flow every wet spring week, yet manhole inspections find the sewers in good shape with little joint leakage.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario village with mostly PVC sewers built in the 1990s; many homes have sump pumps for high groundwater. Records are for training only.

evidence.label: Wet weather flow rises within minutes of rain starting, faster than groundwater infiltration usually responds.
Dye placed in several homes' foundation drains appears at the plant within the hour.
Night flows in dry weather are low and normal, so groundwater infiltration is small.
The extra water arriving is clean and cold, like foundation drainage.
Sections of town built without sump pumps show much smaller wet weather increases.

inference.prompt: What is the best supported inference from these observations?

options.label: Roof leaders and foundation drains connected to the sanitary sewer, including sump pumps, are sending storm water straight into the system.
The PVC sewers are leaking badly at every joint despite appearances.
A creek is overflowing into a manhole somewhere in town.
The plant's influent meter over reads in wet weather.
